II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)


A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

Paul begins the first section of the benediction with a statement that follows the traditional pattern for the opening of a benedictory prayer. God, he says, is praised because of the blessings he has given to his people. These blessings are both spiritual, since they are the gifts of the Spirit, and heavenly, because they exist in a dimension of existence that stands outside everyday experience (v. 3).

Paul describes the first of these blessings in 1:4–6—God has made believers his people as a completely free act of his grace. To express this, Paul uses a complex phrase that states the blessing (he chose believers, v. 4), restates it from a different perspective (he decided in advance to adopt them as his own children, v. 5a), explains the attitude with which God gave believers the blessing (it gave him great pleasure to do this, v. 5b), and then announces the purpose for which he did so (that believers might praise him for his grace, v. 6). God accomplished all this for his people “in Christ” (v. 4; cf. “by means of Jesus Christ” in v. 5 and “in the Beloved” in v. 6).



Exegesis and Exposition

3Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, 4inasmuch as he chose us in him before the foundation of the universe so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love, 5ahaving predestined us for adoptive sonship by means of Jesus Christ, for him[self], 5baccording to the good pleasure of his will, 6for the praise of his glorious grace, ⌜which⌝ he graciously gave us in the ⌜Beloved⌝, . . . .

[1:3] The opening line of Paul’s benediction follows a pattern familiar from Israel’s Scriptures and Jewish literature of the Second Temple period. Often those who bless God do so because God has given blessings (Gen. 24:27, 35, 48; Jdt. 13:18; Tob. 13:17; 4Q404 10). They also often describe God as the God of some great figure of the past such as Abraham or Israel and then state why God should be blessed (e.g., Gen. 24:27; 1 Sam. 25:32; 1 Kings 8:15; 2 Chron. 2:12; 6:4; Ezra 7:27; Ps. 72:18; Dan. 3:28; Luke 1:68). The verbal adjective εὐλογητός (eulogētos), which is uncommon in nonbiblical Greek, means “blessed” in the sense of “praised,” and therefore Paul is saying that God is praised by those whom he has blessed. He is not expressing the wish that God would be blessed or issuing an implicit admonition that he should be blessed, but in a way analogous to his brief benediction in Rom. 1:25 (ὅς ἐστιν εὐλογητός, hos estin eulogētos, who is blessed), Paul is saying that God is blessed and implying that the people whom he blesses are those who bless him.[1]

Outside of Jewish contexts, the verb εὐλογέω (eulogeō) and the noun εὐλογία (eulogia) referred primarily to the praise of people. Εὐλογέω meant “speak well of,” “deliver a panegyric upon,” and εὐλογία referred to “good” or “fine language,” “praise,” “a eulogy,” or “good fame.” The gods could “bless” people, but this meant only that they “honored” them (LSJ 720). Paul’s use of these terms, however, follows the pattern of Biblical Greek where they refer not to the honor that people receive from God but to the good things that God does for them. God blessed Abraham by delivering him from his enemies and giving him wealth (Gen. 14:20; 24:35); God blessed Moses by delivering him from the Egyptians (Exod. 18:10); God blessed Naomi by providing her with next-of-kin (Ruth 4:14); God blessed Judith by allowing her to kill Holofernes (Jdt. 13:18). In the same way, Paul says that God is blessed because he has done good things for the letter’s readers.

Paul describes these blessings with the adjective πνευματικός (pneumatikos, spiritual), a characteristically Pauline term (BDAG 837).[2] Since Paul couples this adjective here with the adjective ἐπουράνιος (epouranios, heavenly) and elsewhere in his letters contrasts “spiritual” people or things with “fleshly” (σαρκικός, sarkikos; σάρκινος, sarkinos; 1 Cor. 3:1, 3; 9:11; Rom. 7:14; 15:27), “physical” (ψυχικός, psychikos; 1 Cor. 15:44, 46), or “human” (ἀνθρώπινος, anthrōpinos; 1 Cor. 2:13) things, many interpreters in the early church, and some in more recent times, have understood “spiritual blessings” to be nonmaterial or otherworldly blessings.[3]

When Paul uses the adjective πνευματικός, however, God’s Spirit almost always stands in the background (see especially 1 Cor. 2:6–3:4). Ephesians 5:19 provides a good example of this: “spiritual songs” are not nonmaterial songs or “religious” as opposed to secular songs, but songs that those filled with God’s Spirit (5:18) sing. Ephesians 6:12 is the one exception to this rule in the Pauline literature. Even here, however, “the spiritual [powers] of evil” who dwell “in the heavenly places” may be related to “the spirit now at work among the sons of disobedience”—probably a reference to the devil—in much the same way that elsewhere “spiritual” persons and things are related to the Spirit of God (Fee 1994: 28–32). “Spiritual blessings,” therefore, are the benefits that come as gracious gifts from the Spirit of God and that Paul describes in 1:4–14 (Aletti 2001: 56).

We learn more about the nature of these “spiritual blessings” when Paul describes them as ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις (en tois epouraniois, in the heavenly places) and ἐν Χριστῷ (en christō, in Christ). In the NT outside of Ephesians, ἐπουράνιος (epouranios, heavenly) is always associated with God and often stands in contrast to what is earthly and therefore less permanent or significant (John 3:12; 1 Cor. 15:48–49; Heb. 8:5; 11:16; 12:18–22; cf. Phil. 2:10). In Ephesians, Paul uses the term in a slightly different way. It appears only in the phrase ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, which occurs nowhere else in the NT and means “in the heavenly places” (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). God and the ascended Christ dwell in the heavenly places in Ephesians, but so do “the spiritual powers of evil” (1:20; 6:12; cf. 3:10).[4] Here, then, the phrase refers to the location or, perhaps better, the “dimension” of existence in which believers experience “every spiritual blessing” (W. H. Harris 1991: 74, 86–87, citing Hanson 1980: 138).

The phrase ἐν Χριστῷ refers even more specifically to the place where these blessings are found. They belong to those who are within the boundaries marked out by the living Christ. It is in this realm that hearing the gospel, believing the gospel, and being sealed with the Holy Spirit take place (1:13). This is the realm in which people experience the same life-giving power of God that raised Christ from the dead and gave him victory over all God’s enemies (1:19–23).

When we put all this together, we find Paul beginning his benedictory prayer with a statement that God is praised among the people whom his Spirit blesses in every possible way. These blessings occur in a dimension of existence that is beyond common, everyday experience, and they belong to those who are united with Christ by their faith in the gospel.

[1:4] Paul uses the term καθώς (kathōs, inasmuch as) to link his opening blessing of God with an account of the specific ways God has blessed those who bless him. This adverbial conjunction normally introduces a comparison, although it can also indicate cause (BDAG 493–94; Wallace 1996: 674–75). Paul can certainly use it in the causal sense (Rom. 1:28; 1 Cor. 1:6; 5:7; Phil. 1:7), and something of that idea probably stands in the background here, but notions of comparison are probably uppermost in his mind. God has blessed believers not only because he chose them but also “inasmuch as” or “to the extent that” he has given them these blessings in all their extravagance (vv. 7b–8a; cf. Ellicott 1859: 6; Eadie, 1883: 18; Schlier 1957: 48–49).

Paul begins his description of God’s blessings by saying that God “chose us” (ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς, exelexato hēmas). Grammatically, this is the only verb in vv. 3–14 that is not subordinate to some other element (Hoehner 2002: 175), and although grammatical priority does not always translate into conceptual priority, it probably does so here. Conceptually, Paul considers God’s free choice of his people to be the clearest indicator of the lavish nature of his grace, as the frequent repetition of the theme of God’s gracious initiative in blessing his people shows (cf. vv. 5, 9, 11).

God’s choice of his people is a traditional Jewish idea, with roots firmly planted in Israel’s Scriptures: “It is you the LORD has chosen out of all the peoples on earth to be his people, his treasured possession” (Deut. 14:2 NRSV; cf. Isa. 43:10). Nothing in Israel, such as the size of the nation or its righteousness, prompted God to choose them as his people (Deut. 7:7; 9:4, 6), but only his love for them (Deut. 7:8; Isa. 44:2 LXX; cf. 41:8 LXX). The idea of God’s elective love for his people was important to Paul. Elsewhere in his correspondence, he emphasizes that God did not choose his people because of some merit in them (Rom. 9:11–12; 1 Cor. 1:27–29; 2 Tim. 1:9; Titus 1:1–2; cf. Cambier 1963: 68), and he links God’s choice of his people with his love for them (Rom. 8:33–39; 1 Thess. 1:4).

Here Paul focuses the attention of his readers on the completely unmerited, gracious nature of God’s choice of believers to be his people with two adverbial prepositional phrases: ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him) and πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (pro katabolēs kosmou, before the foundation of the world; Calvin 1965: 125). He describes the purpose of God’s choice with another adverbial phrase, εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ (einai hēmas hagious kai amōmous katenōpion autou en agapē, that we might be holy and blameless before him in love). The phrase ἐν αὐτῷ probably does not refer to the preexistence of Christ, in whom believers were chosen before the foundation of the world (as Pokorný 1992: 57, among many others, argues), but functions in the same way that the phrase διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (dia Iēsou Christou, through Jesus Christ) works in the next clause (v. 5a): it describes the means by which God’s choice became effective for believers (Oecumenius, PG 118:1173; Cambier 1963: 69–71). This happened through Christ’s death on their behalf (v. 7a), which was a lavish demonstration of the grace of God (vv. 6–7b; cf. Hoehner 2002: 177).

The phrase καταβολὴ κόσμου was a common expression in Second Temple Judaism and early Christianity for God’s creation of the world (e.g., Matt. 25:34; Luke 11:50; John 17:24; Heb. 4:3; 1 Pet. 1:20; Rev. 13:8; T. Mos. 1.14; Barn. 5.5), and the idea that God chose his people before the world’s foundation was well known (Matt. 25:34; Rev. 17:8; T. Mos. 1.12–14; cf. Jub. 2.20; Jos. Asen. 8.9; Hofius 1971: 123–28; Aune 1998: 748–49). Although he does not say so explicitly, Paul probably uses the phrase here to emphasize the graciousness of God’s choice: it happened before believers could do anything to effect it, and therefore it came as an absolutely free gift (Calvin 1965: 125; Best 1998: 120; O’Brien 1999: 100). This understanding of the phrase meshes with the emphasis of the benediction on the extravagance of God’s grace (vv. 6, 7b) and with the link that Paul makes elsewhere in his letters between God’s choice of his people before they existed, on one hand, and God’s mercy or grace, on the other hand (Rom. 9:11; 2 Tim. 1:9; cf. 1 Cor. 1:26–31).[5]

God chose believers so that they might be ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ (hagious kai amōmous katenōpion autou en agapē, holy and blameless before him in love). Here too Paul uses the traditional language of election. According to Deuteronomy, the Lord’s choice of Israel “out of all the peoples on earth” as his people meant they should be “holy”—separated by their behavior from the peoples who surrounded them in the land. They must take precautions not to fall under the influence of the idolatrous customs of the indigenous peoples because God’s choice of Israel as his own people has set them apart: “For you are a people holy [LXX ἅγιος, hagios] to the LORD your God; the LORD your God has chosen you out of all the peoples of the earth to be his people, his treasured possession” (Deut. 7:1–6 NRSV; cf. 14:1–2). God has separated them from other nations by lovingly choosing them, and them alone; now they are to act in ways that God describes in his law to show their separate status as his chosen and treasured possession (cf. Quell, TDNT 4:163–64).

Paul follows the term “holy” with a word often used in the LXX rendering of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Ezekiel to refer to the “unblemished” (ἄμωμος, amōmos) animal that the worshiper should bring in sacrifice to God (e.g., Exod. 29:1, 38; Lev. 1:3, 10; Num. 6:14). The LXX also often uses the term metaphorically of both people and God, to mean “morally blameless” or “perfect” (e.g., 2 Sam. 22:24, 31; Ps. 15:2 [14:2 LXX]), and this is how Paul uses it here. His use of the phrase κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ (katenōpion autou, before him) probably means that the metaphor of an unblemished sacrifice to God was not entirely dead for Paul since the rare term κατενώπιον also appears in a genuinely cultic context in Lev. 4:17 (cf. Best 1998: 121).[6]

How Paul intended his readers to take the next phrase is not entirely clear. Many interpreters believe that ἐν ἀγάπῃ (en agapē, in love) does not describe more specifically the holy and blameless behavior that should characterize God’s chosen people (“holy and blameless before him in love”) but is an adverbial qualifier of προορίσας (proorisas, having predestined), the participle that begins verse 5 (“having predestined us in love”). A simple pause for breath in the right place would have easily resolved the ambiguity in the original dictation of the letter, but the ambiguity remains in the written text (cf. the comments on 2:14–15; 3:17b).

Those who take ἐν ἀγάπῃ with προορίσας point out that Paul’s focus in the benediction is on God’s action of blessing his people, not on human obligation, and that a sudden, brief admonition to live in a holy and blameless way would disrupt this focus (Caragounis 1977: 85). They also argue that the terms “holy” and “blameless” are cultic terms describing the consecration and condition of a sacrificial animal placed “before” God. These terms refer not to the conduct of believers, therefore, but to the status believers have in God’s sight (Best 1998: 123).

Two considerations, however, weigh against these arguments. First, although it is true that Paul conceived of God as conferring a status of holiness on believers when he chose them to be his people, the biblical passages that form the background to Paul’s concept view the gift of holiness as, at the same time, a call to act in the holy ways that God prescribes. The two ideas were tied together in Deut. 7:1–6 and 14:1–2, and they were tied together for Paul. He could tell the Corinthians, for example, that they were “sanctified [ἁγιάζω, hagiazō] in Christ Jesus” and that they “had been sanctified [ἁγιάζω, hagiazō],” and yet he could call on them to “bring about” their “sanctification [ἁγιωσύνη, hagiōsynē] in the fear of God” (1 Cor. 1:2; 6:11; 2 Cor. 7:1). It is likely that this understanding of holiness also lies beneath his use of this language in Eph. 1:4.

Second, the sentence structure of verses 3–14 makes it likely that ἐν ἀγάπῃ does not qualify the participle that follows it. Wherever Paul uses a verbal form in the benediction to describe the action of God and then qualifies that verbal form with a prepositional phrase, the qualifying phrase always comes after the verbal form, not before it. This makes it unlikely that ἐν ἀγάπῃ would qualify προορίσας, which follows it.[7]

None of this means that God did not predetermine believers “in love” for adoptive status as his children. As we have seen, the biblical background of the concept of election is steeped in the notion that God loves those whom he chooses. Paul expresses that idea in this passage, however, through the language of God’s “good pleasure” (εὐδοκία, eudokia) in predetermining the adoptive sonship of his people (v. 5) and in planning in advance to sum up all things in Christ (vv. 9–10).

The attachment of the phrase ἐν ἀγάπῃ to “holy” and “blameless” means that in this benediction Paul anticipates the concrete ethical exhortation that he gives later in the letter (4:1–6:20). Paul begins that part of the letter by urging his readers to live in a way that is “worthy of the calling [κλήσεως, klēseōs] with which you were called [ἐκλήθητε, eklēthēte]” and then specifies that they should bear with one another “in love” (ἐν ἀγάπῃ; 4:1–2; cf. 4:15–16; 5:2, 25, 28, 33; 6:23). Although the focus of the benediction lies on what God has graciously done for his people, then, here Paul hints at what he will say more fully in the letter’s second half: God’s action on his readers’ behalf has implications for the way they should live.

[1:5a] Paul next uses the aorist participle προορίσας (proorisas, having predestined) to describe God’s choice more fully. Just as the preposition πρό (pro, before) in 1:4 placed God’s choice of his people before his creation of the world, so Paul prefixed this preposition to the verb ὁρίζω (horizō, determine) to place God’s decision to mark off a people for himself chronologically before the world began. Did Paul think there was a difference between God’s choice of his people before the world’s creation and God’s delimiting his people before the world’s creation? If not, then the statement certainly seems redundant (Hoehner 2002: 194). Perhaps, therefore, we should take the aorist tense of the participle to refer to antecedent time and understand Paul to say that God predestined his people and then chose them (Alford 1857: 69; Ellicott 1859: 7–8; cf. Rom. 8:28–30). Alternatively, perhaps προορίσας states the cause of God’s choice: he chose his people because he determined beforehand that they would be his people (Hodge 1856: 37; Lightfoot 1895: 315; Abbott 1897: 8; Hoehner 2002: 194).

If Paul were engaged in a philosophical discussion about the precise logic of election (cf. Calvin 1997: 113–20), and if Ephesians demonstrated an economy of language that made redundancy improbable, one of these explanations might be correct. Paul’s focus, however, is not on the logic of election but on its occurrence and the need to praise God because his choice of a people for himself is such a clear demonstration of his grace. Paul’s use of language in Ephesians generally, and in this benediction particularly, moreover, is as lavish in its own way as the grace of God, which he praises. Redundancy, then, is not a valid objection to understanding προορίσας ἡμᾶς as a restatement of ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς. Paul simply turns the jewel slightly and views it from a different angle, now describing God’s primordial action on behalf of his people not as his choice but as his predetermination of them. God determined that they would be his people before the foundation of the world. Their status as his people, therefore, came as an utterly free gift, irrespective of anything they could possibly have done to merit it.

This shift in perspective also means that Paul now changes his angle of vision on God’s purpose in predetermining who his people would be. Though in 1:4 Paul had said that God’s purpose in election was that they might be holy and blameless before him in love, he now describes God’s purpose in predetermining his people as their “adoptive sonship” (υἱοθεσίαν, huiothesian).[8] In the Greek Bible, this is a distinctively Pauline term. It is never used in the LXX, and in the NT it appears only here and in Gal. 4:5; Rom. 8:15, 23; and 9:4. The term was common, however, in the Greco-Roman world, where it referred to a legal practice by which the father of a family accepted as his heir a male child who was not his own. Paul must have known that his Gentile readers in Roman Asia would hear resonances of this practice in the term (cf. J. Scott 1992: 3–57, 267), but his use of it to describe one of the privileges of national Israel in Rom. 9:4 means that he probably also had in mind biblical ideas of Israel’s “sonship” (Byrne 1979: 79–84).

Both the OT and Jewish literature of the Second Temple period claim that God’s people Israel are his “sons” (LXX υἱοί, huioi: Deut. 14:1; Isa. 1:2; 30:9; Hos. 1:10 [2:1 MT, LXX]; Wis. 12:21; 16:26), his “children” (LXX τέκνα, tekna: Deut. 32:5; Isa. 63:8; Wis. 16:21), or comprise his “firstborn son” (Exod. 4:22–23; Jer. 31:9; Sir. 36:17; cf. Wis. 18:13; Jub. 2.20; 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 6:58; 4Q504 3.6–7; cf. Hos. 11:1). This relationship had become strained through Israel’s rebellion (Deut. 32:5, 19; Isa. 1:2; 30:1) but would one day be fully restored in the eschatological age (e.g., Isa. 63:8–9; Hos. 1:10 [2:1 MT, LXX]; Jub. 1.24–25; Sib. Or. 3.702–9). Paul believed that the presence of God’s Spirit among believers was evidence that this time of eschatological restoration had begun, that believers were God’s children, that they were now spiritually related to Jesus—God’s Son par excellence—and that they were heirs with him of a future glory when their bodily resurrection would make their “adoptive sonship” complete (Gal. 4:1–7; Rom. 8:14–17; cf. 2 Cor. 6:18).[9]

This is the light in which we should understand Paul’s claim that God predestined the adoptive sonship of believers διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (dia Iēsou Christou). Adoption as God’s children is theirs “through Jesus Christ” because through their union with him, Jesus Christ shares his divine sonship with them. Believers call God “Abba Father” because Jesus spoke this way of his relationship with God (Gal. 4:6; Rom. 8:15; cf. Mark 14:36 and Jeremias 1971: 61–68). They are heirs of God because Jesus is God’s heir (Gal. 4:7; Rom. 8:17). His status as God’s Son lifts them out of the status of slaves and makes them sons and daughters of God with him (Gal. 3:23–4:7; Rom. 8:15–17).

Paul expresses the goal of all this in the phrase εἰς αὐτόν (eis auton, to him). The αὐτόν here could refer to either Christ or God. Later in the letter Paul speaks of Christians arriving “at a mature man” (εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον, eis andra teleion), a man whom he identifies as Christ (4:13). He then urges his readers to “grow up to him” (εἰς αὐτόν), again referring to Christ (4:15).[10] It is more likely, however, that 1:4–5 follows the same pattern of stating the action of God (choosing/predetermining), the purpose for the action (to be holy and blameless in love/to be adopted children), and the divine goal of the action (before/to God). With this prepositional phrase, therefore, Paul is saying that the goal of the adoptive sonship of believers is a relationship with God similar to that of Jesus’s own filial relationship with God. The adoptive sonship of believers is εἰς αὐτόν, oriented toward God.[11]

[1:5b–6] Paul next uses two prepositional phrases to describe the attitude with which God predetermined that he would adopt believers as his own children and the purpose for which he would do so. His attitude was one of deep desire, of good pleasure (εὐδοκία, eudokia; cf., e.g., Ps. 144:16 LXX [145:16 MT, Eng.]; Rom. 10:1). Paul was not content to say simply that God predestined believers to be his people κατὰ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ (kata to thelēma autou, according to his will). He said instead that God’s will in this matter expressed what he took great pleasure in doing (cf. Barth 1974: 81; Best 1998: 126–27). He determined in advance that those who are in Christ would be his people κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ (kata tēn eudokian tou thelēmatos autou, according to the good pleasure of his will).

The purpose for which he predestined believers to be his adoptive children is related to this attitude. He did this for the praise “of his glorious grace, which he graciously gave us in the Beloved” (δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, doxēs tēs charitos autou ēs echaritōsen hēmas en tō ēgapēmenō). The string of genitive nouns and pronouns that Paul uses to express this thought is typical of the letter’s style in its first half. Where they occur, these genitive strings slow the discourse and emphasize the grandeur or gravity of the thought (1:18b, 19b; 2:2b, 20b; 3:7; 4:13 [2x]). Here the phrase δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς . . . (doxēs tēs charitos autou hēs . . . , of his glorious grace, which . . .) reins in the discourse of the benediction and allows the reader, or those hearing the letter read aloud, to savor this final thought of the benediction’s first major part. God took pleasure in his primordial decision to adopt believers as his children, and he did this so that they might praise him for the magnificence of his grace.

God graciously granted believers his grace ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (en tō ēgapēmenō, in the Beloved). Here Paul picks up the thought of the ἐν Χριστῷ (en Christō, in Christ) in 1:3, the ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him) in 1:4, and the διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (dia Iēsou Christou, through Jesus Christ) in 1:5 and thus provides a transition to the benediction’s second part, where he explains precisely how God showed believers his grace in Christ (vv. 7–10). The name that he uses for Christ is significant. The Scriptures and Second Temple Jewish literature speak of especially important individuals in Israel’s history, such as Abraham (LXX: 2 Chron. 20:7; Pr. Azar. 12), Moses (Sir. 45:1), and Solomon (Neh. 13:26), as “beloved” of God, and so it is not unexpected when, in the Synoptic Gospels, God calls Jesus his “Beloved” (Matt. 3:17; 12:18; 17:5; Mark 1:11; 9:7; 12:6; Luke 3:22; 20:13).[12] Ancient Jewish literature also speaks of the nation Israel as God’s “beloved” (e.g., Isa. 5:1; Jer. 11:15; 12:7; Bar. 3:36 [3:37 LXX]; Jdt. 9:4), and the LXX translators consistently translated the name “Jeshurun,” a biblical term of endearment for Israel, with the word “beloved” (Deut. 32:15; 33:5, 26; Isa. 44:2). In Matthew’s paraphrase of Isa. 42:1–4, the concepts of God’s election, his good pleasure, and his beloved all converge, much as they do in Eph. 1:4–6, and Matthew applies all of this to Jesus (Matt. 12:18–20). In its original context in Isaiah, however, it is unclear whether the passage refers to the nation Israel or to an individual within Israel as a representative of the nation.

Paul’s use of the term “beloved” reflects this same alternation between a chosen and “beloved” individual and God’s chosen and “beloved” people. He knew the early Christian tradition that Jesus was God’s Beloved (Col. 1:13), and he frequently called God’s people God’s beloved (1 Thess. 1:4; 2 Thess. 2:13; Rom. 9:25; Col. 3:12; Eph. 5:1), sometimes in combination with the claim that God’s people are his “elect” (1 Thess. 1:4). It seems likely, therefore, that when Paul calls Jesus “the Beloved” in this passage he has in mind Jesus’s embodiment within himself of the beloved and elect people of God (cf. Caird 1976: 36; Lincoln 1990: 26–27; O’Brien 1999: 105). God has shown believers his praiseworthy grace, therefore, not merely “by means of the Beloved,” through his atoning death, but also “in the Beloved,” through their identification with Christ.

God’s delight in this act of free and lavish grace toward believers prompt them to praise him, and the praise of his people for his grace was the ultimate purpose of his primordial decision to make believers his people. With this thought, Paul brings the first part of his benediction to a close and prepares his readers for its second major section.

Summary

Paul begins his benediction by announcing its theme: he intends to praise God for the good things God has done for those who have been united with Christ by their faith in the gospel. These blessings come through the work of the Spirit and are experienced in the dimension of existence where God and all the cosmic powers dwell.

After this general statement of praise, Paul begins to give examples of all the blessings that God has given to those who are in Christ. The first section of the prayer explores the blessing that God chose those who are in Christ. His choice came to them as an utterly free gift, accomplished before they even existed, and it placed them, like Israel and even Jesus himself, within God’s family. God adopted them as his children, and this was something he took great pleasure in doing. God did all this, moreover, with at least two purposes in mind: he wanted a people who would be separate from the world around them both in their dedication to him and in their love for one another, and he wanted a people who would praise him for the glorious grace he had shown them in his Beloved Son. Exactly how God showed them grace in his Son will form the subject of the benedictory prayer’s next section.



Additional Notes

1:6. Instead of τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς, many manuscripts (אi2, D, G, K, L, Ψ, most cursives), versions (itd, itg, vg, syrh, goth), and ancient commentators (Theodoret, John of Damascus, Photius, and Oecumenius) have τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἐν ᾗ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς. At least one modern commentator (Hoehner 2002: 202) has also adopted this as the correct reading.

The difference in meaning between ἐν ᾗ and the relative pronoun ἧς here is so slight that it is difficult to capture it in English translation, but the prepositional phrase, if it is original, lends itself more easily to the interpretation that God bestowed upon believers a gracious disposition. It could be taken to mean that “he made us gracious by his grace” rather than that “he gave us his grace.”[13] Chrysostom, although he read ἧς, took the text in this direction in his comments on it, claiming that God had bestowed upon believers the favor of making them lovely people (Hom. Eph., hom. 1; NPNF 13:52–53).[14]

The reading ἐν ᾗ, however, is probably not what Paul wrote, for two reasons. First, the witnesses to the simple relative pronoun ἧς (𝔓46, א*, A, B, P, 0278, 6, 33, 81, 88, 330, 365, 424c, 436, 1175, 1319, 1739, 1837, 1881, 1908, 2127, 2464) include the earliest manuscripts of Ephesians and some early commentators (Origen, Chrysostom, and Euthalius). Second, as the occurrence of the same construction later in verses 7–8 shows (τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐπερίσσευσεν), the reading with ἧς is consistent with the style of the letter. It is not likely, moreover, that a scribe conformed an original ἐν ᾗ in verse 6 to the ἧς of verses 7b–8a, since the ἧς of verse 6 comes first in the text.

1:6. Some ancient uncial manuscripts (D*, F, G) and versions (a number of Old Latin manuscripts, the 1592 Clementine edition of the Vulgate, Thomas of Harkel’s Syriac edition, Sahidic and Ethiopic versions), and some church fathers (e.g., Adamantius, Theodotus of Ancyra, Victorinus of Rome, “Ambrosiaster,” Pelagius, and Augustine) read the words υἱῷ αὐτοῦ after ἠγαπημένῳ. This is very weak support. It is both late chronologically and mostly limited to the Western text type (cf. Metzger 1968: 214; Hoehner 2002: 203n3). The vast majority of manuscripts, including the oldest and most conservative witnesses, omit the phrase, and so there is no real debate over its authenticity.

How did the variant arise? A similar phrase appears in Col. 1:13 (ὁ ὑιὸς τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ), and a scribe may have inadvertently supplied the extra words from that source or from the frequent appearance of similar expressions elsewhere in the New Testament (cf. Mark 1:11; 9:7; 12:6; Matt. 3:17; 17:5; Luke 3:22; 20:13; 2 Pet. 1:17).





II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)


B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

The second main part of the benediction praises God for two further blessings he has lavished on his people. First, Paul praises God for the specific way in which he freely granted grace to his people in the Beloved (cf. v. 6b). He did this through a rescue effort not unlike the redemption of his people from slavery in Egypt and his restoration of them to the land after the Babylonian exile. In this case, however, the redemption was not rescue from literal slavery or exile, but rescue from transgressions. Rescue from transgressions did not merely involve overcoming the enemies of his people, but also forgiveness. This forgiveness was extraordinarily costly: it was bought with the price of the violent death of God’s Beloved Son (1:7a).

Paul takes God’s willingness to pay this price as a demonstration that he was not simply gracious to believers but overwhelmingly gracious (vv. 7b–8). They have experienced redemption and forgiveness, Paul says, because God’s grace is vast, because he took the initiative to show it to them, and because he did this “in all wisdom and understanding.” It was not an ill-considered or haphazard rescue operation but part of a purposely designed plan that accords with his essential character. God’s nature is not merely to be gracious, but also to be lavishly gracious to his people.

Second, Paul praises God because he showed his abundant grace to his people by revealing to them “the mystery of his will” (v. 9). God planned to do this in Christ and took pleasure in doing it. Here too, therefore, Paul emphasizes that God’s revelation of his will to his people was not something he gave grudgingly, nor anything that his people had a right to because of their upright behavior. God revealed his purposes to his people as part of his design for the unfolding of history (v. 10a).

The mystery itself is God’s arrangement of “the times” in order to sum up all things, whether heavenly or earthly, in Christ. When Christ’s work is complete, the unfolding of history will make sense: all creatures that have ever lived, whether in heaven or on earth, will take the place that God intended them to have with respect to Christ (v. 10b). What has happened in the past will make sense in light of the future that Christ will bring.



Exegesis and Exposition

7a. . . in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of transgressions, 7b–8according to the wealth of his grace, which he lavished on us in all wisdom and understanding, 9by making known to us the ⌜mystery⌝ of his will according to his good pleasure, which he planned in him 10for administering the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, things in the heavens and things on the earth in him, . . .

[1:7a] Paul now describes what God has graciously done for believers in Christ with a new metaphor, and he goes into greater detail about what precisely Christ did. The ἐν ᾧ (en hō, in whom) continues the thought of ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (en tō ēgapēmenō, in the Beloved) in the previous verse and should not, therefore, be translated “by whom” but “in whom”: God made believers his people through their identification with Christ (Abbott 1897: 11; Best 1998: 129; Hoehner 2002: 205; pace Calvin 1965: 127; Alford 1857: 71). Paul now describes how God did this with the help of the new metaphor of redemption. By their identification with him, he says, believers have τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ (tēn apolytrōsin dia tou haimatos autou, redemption through his blood). The term ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis) appears only ten times in the NT and is rare in Greek literature predating the NT. Its one use in the LXX (Dan. 4:34) appears in a passage with no corresponding Hebrew text and seems to mean “deliverance.”[1] In one of two uses of the verbal form ἀπολυτρόω in the LXX, the meaning, similarly, is “deliver” (Zeph. 3:1). When the noun appears in nonbiblical Greek, however, it has the more specific meaning of either “holding for ransom” (Plutarch, Pomp. 24.2) or “paying a ransom” (Josephus, Ant. 12.27) and was used to refer to the freeing of slaves through the payment of a price (Let. Arist. 12, 33; Philo, Good Person 114). This seems to be the meaning of the other of the two uses of the verb in the LXX (Exod. 21:8).

A heated debate has surrounded the issue of whether ἀπολύτρωσις, when it appears in the NT, refers specifically to God’s purchase of people from captivity to sin at the cost of Christ’s death (e.g., Morris 1955: 37–48; Ridderbos 1975: 193–97), or more generally to God’s deliverance of people from the plight into which sin has plunged them (e.g., Abbott 1897: 11–13; Büchsel, TDNT 4:351–56; D. Hill 1967: 71–76).

When the debate reaches our text, those on one side see the phrase διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ (dia tou haimatos autou, through his blood) as a reference to the price that Christ paid for our redemption (Morris 1955: 38–41; Ridderbos 1975: 194; Hoehner 2002: 205–6), and those on the other side of the debate respond that διά followed by the genitive case only describes the means through which the deliverance was accomplished and does not specify a redemption price. If Paul had intended to speak of a redemption price, he would have simply used the genitive case (“the genitive of price”) without an intervening preposition (D. Hill 1967: 73; Best 1998: 130; cf. Lincoln 1990: 28).[2]

This debate is so vigorous because the doctrinal issues that lie beneath it are important. Those who insist that Paul understood the term to signify the payment of a price are interested in protecting a classic Christian understanding of the way in which Christ atoned for sin (Morris 1955: 58, 275–80). Photius, the ninth-century patriarch of Constantinople, puts it this way in his comment on this text: “[God’s beloved Son] himself effected the redemption for us. For we were prisoners because of our transgressions, but by giving his blood as a ransom [λύτρον, lytron] for us he ransomed [ἐλυτρώσατο, elytrōsato] us from the tyranny in which we were being held” (my trans.; text in Staab 1933: 611).[3] Behind this comment seems to lie the notion that transgression against God’s law incurs a debt that must be paid for justice to be satisfied, and death is the currency in which it must be paid. To spare the lives of his people, Christ died for them, thus paying the necessary penalty. Those who believe that notions of a payment price do not inform the use of the term here, and in most of its other uses in the NT, are sometimes suspicious that the other side has forced its preconceived dogmatic concerns on unwilling texts, including Eph. 1:7 (e.g., D. Hill 1967: 69).

In evaluating the evidence, it seems first of all necessary to clear the theological air by observing that the NT unambiguously describes the blood of Christ as the ransom price for sinners. This is implied by the most natural readings of 1 Pet. 1:18–19; Heb. 9:12; Rev. 1:5; 5:9 (Lightfoot 1895: 316; cf. Best 1998: 130). Unlike some later theologians, the authors of these NT texts seem uninterested in identifying the person to whom the price was paid and precisely why, in legal terms, a payment price was necessary.[4] The basic notion that transgression results in a plight analogous to captivity or slavery—and that Christ’s death has satisfied the conditions for release from that captivity and thus paid the necessary ransom—is unambiguously a biblical idea.

It seems likely, moreover, that in Eph. 1:7 Paul’s Greek-speaking readers in western Asia would have most readily understood the term ἀπολύτρωσις as a metaphorical reference to the price paid to buy the freedom of a captive or slave and would have understood the phrase διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ as a reference to the purchase price. The expression would perhaps have seemed odd to them—something like saying in English, “I bought the bread with five dollars” rather than “for five dollars”—but the use of the term ἀπολύτρωσις (or one of its cognates) for slave redemption would have been so familiar to them that it is hard to imagine they did not take the phrase in this way. Ancient Greek-speaking interpreters of Eph. 1:7 do not hesitate to take it this way.[5] Paul was probably aware that his readers would understand the phrase as a metaphorical reference to the redemption of slaves or captives and must have been happy with the meaning of Christ’s death that he knew the phrase would convey to them.

At the same time, Paul probably appreciated, and hoped that some of his readers would appreciate, the biblical overtones of this word. The noun ἀπολύτρωσις is closely related to the verb λυτρόω (lytroō, ransom), which the LXX translators used to render two Hebrew verbs, גָּאַל (gāʾal) and פָּדָה (pādâ), both of which also mean “redeem” (HALOT 1:169; 2:911–12). In both the Hebrew Scriptures and the LXX, all three terms and the nouns associated with them frequently carry a metaphorical meaning, distinctive to Biblical Greek, in which the notion of a purchase price fades into the background and the simple notion of deliverance or rescue, whether from Egypt, Babylon, other nations, or personal distress, becomes primary. Exodus 6:6 LXX provides a good example of this use of the verb λυτρόω: “I am the Lord, and I will bring you out, away from the domination of the Egyptians, and I will deliver [ῥύσομαι, rhysomai] you from slavery, and I will redeem [λυτρώσομαι, lytrōsomai] you by a raised arm and great judgment” (NETS).[6] It is difficult to understand God’s raised arm and great judgment against the Egyptians as a “price” that God pays for the redemption of his people from slavery. As the parallel verb ῥύσομαι shows, the notion of simple rescue is the chief meaning here.

Paul probably intended his use of the similar word ἀπολύτρωσις in Eph. 1:7 to carry primarily these overtones of God’s great deliverance of his people for their sins. This primary concern accounts for his use of the term in a similar phrase in Col. 1:14, where the reference to Christ’s blood as the “cost” of redemption does not appear.[7] It also accounts better for the broadening of the word in Eph. 1:14 and 4:30 to include the consummation of God’s saving purposes for his people in the future, a broadening that seems to leave notions of the payment of a redemption price behind (cf. Zeph. 3:1 LXX; Luke 21:28; Rom. 8:23).

To summarize, Paul’s use of the phrase τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ probably means that the metaphor of redemption from slavery through the payment of a price was alive for him. It is unlikely that he failed to realize that this meaning would occur readily to his Gentile readers and, therefore, unlikely that he did not intend to communicate this meaning. Paul’s primary concern in using the metaphor, however, was probably to communicate that in the death of Christ, God came powerfully to the rescue of his people just as he had done in former times when he rescued them from the Egyptians, the Babylonians, and other nations. Paul saw this climactic rescue effort, accomplished through the death of his Beloved Son Jesus Christ, as a measure of God’s lavish grace.

Paul explains the meaning of this metaphor by placing his next phrase in apposition to τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν. The redemption of believers, he says, entailed τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν παραπτωμάτων (tēn aphesin tōn paraptōmatōn, the forgiveness of transgressions). The term ἄφεσις (aphesis, forgiveness) appears only twice in the Pauline corpus (here and in Col. 1:14), and its verbal form ἀφίημι (aphiēmi) appears only once in the sense of “forgive” (Rom. 4:7). Paul sometimes also uses the term χαρίζομαι (charizomai) to mean “forgive” (2 Cor. 2:7, 10; 12:13; Eph. 4:32; Col. 2:13; 3:13), but words for forgiveness, especially God’s forgiveness, are not prominent in his letters. In speaking of divine forgiveness, Paul uses them only in Colossians (2:13; 3:13) and Ephesians (4:32) and once in Romans (4:7), in a quotation of Ps. 31:1 LXX (32:1 MT, Eng.). The concept of forgiveness figures more prominently in Paul’s theology, however, than a simple word count reveals. In Rom. 4:7–8 Paul defines God’s willingness to “reckon” faith as “righteousness” and his willingness not to “reckon” (λογίζομαι) sin against a person in terms of God’s willingness to forgive that person’s sins. This concept probably is also present, therefore, when Paul says in 2 Cor. 5:19 that in Christ, God “was reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning [λογιζόμενος, logizomenos] their transgressions against them.” Paul’s language of justification and reconciliation, therefore, probably includes for him the notion that God forgives sin.

Here Paul makes explicit what is usually latent elsewhere: God’s people presently have forgiveness for their sins because God, at the high cost of the death of his Beloved Son, has rescued them from the plight of alienation from himself into which their sins had plunged them (cf. Eph. 2:1–3, 5a, 16b; 4:18; 5:8a). Paul will later say that the redemption of God’s people is not yet complete (1:14; 4:30), but here his focus remains on what God has already done for believers and on the present effects of what he has done (cf. Rom. 5:1–2a).

[1:7b–8] Paul emphasizes the high cost at which God has purchased forgiveness for believers as a way of demonstrating to his readers the extravagance with which God has lavished his grace on them. The phrase κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ (kata to ploutos tēs charitos autou, according to the wealth of his grace) modifies the present tense verb ἔχομεν (echomen, we have) to show that the present blessing of the forgiveness of their sins results from the abundance of God’s grace. The relative clause that follows the phrase (v. 8a) and qualifies the term χάριτος makes the same point.[8] God did not merely show believers grace when he forgave them at such great cost to himself; he also “caused” grace “to abound” toward them (ἐπερίσσευσεν, eperisseusen; BDAG 805) or “lavished” it on them.

Most interpreters take the next phrase, ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει (en pasē sophia kai phronēsei, in all wisdom and understanding), as a further description of what God lavishes on his people. He not only makes his grace abound toward them, but along with his grace he also gives them wisdom and understanding. This way of taking the phrase is consistent with Paul’s prayer reports elsewhere in Ephesians and Colossians. There Paul says that he prays for God to give his readers “the Spirit of wisdom [σοφίας, sophias] and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Eph. 1:17–18) and that God will fill them “with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and insight [ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ συνέσει πνευματικῇ, en pasē sophia kai synesei pneumatikē]” (Col. 1:9).[9]

A persistent minority of commentators from ancient times to the present, however, has insisted that at this point in the letter the phrase ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει must refer to God’s wisdom and understanding.[10] Those who read the phrase this way often point out that it reflects a typically Jewish way of speaking about God (e.g., Jer. 10:12; 51:15; Ps. 104:24; Prov. 3:19; Sir. 1:1; 1QS 4.18; 1QHa 9.7, 14, 19; 17.17, 23; Origen [Heine 2002: 93–94]; Gnilka 1971: 71; Best 1998: 132; Sellin 2008: 99). They also observe that it is the most natural way to take the Greek, although they then part company and construe the Greek in two different ways. Some observe that the direct object of the verb ἐπερίσσευσεν is the relative pronoun ἧς, attracted out of the accusative and into the genitive case by its antecedent χάριτος. The relative pronoun, therefore, makes the expression complete: God lavishes grace on believers. There is no need to bring wisdom and understanding into the picture to complete the meaning of ἐπερίσσευσεν (Gnilka 1971: 77; Best 1998: 133). The phrase ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει goes instead with the participle γνωρίσας (gnōrisas, making known) in verse 9 to describe how God made the mystery known to believers. He made the mystery known to them in a manner consistent with his great wisdom and understanding.

Others believe that ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει goes with the ἐπερίσσευσεν in the immediately preceding clause and means that God has lavished his grace on believers in all wisdom and understanding (Jerome [Heine 2002: 95]; Alford 1857: 73; Simpson 1957: 31; cf. Origen [Heine 2002: 94–95]).[11] In defense of taking the phrase this way, Alford observes the similarity between the Greek of verse 6b and the Greek of verse 8 (1857: 73). In verse 6b, Paul writes of the grace ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ (hēs echaritōsen hēmas en tō ēgapēmenō, which he graciously gave us in the Beloved). Here the ἐν (en, in) clause does not supply the object of God’s giving—that is contained in the genitive relative pronoun ἧς (hēs, which)—but it functions as an adverbial modifier of ἐχαρίτωσεν (echaritōsen, he graciously gave) and describes the sphere in which, and the means by which, God gave us his grace. He did so “in the Beloved.” By analogy, then, the phrase ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει should modify the verb ἐπερίσσευσεν and tell believers how God lavished his grace upon them: he did so in his multifaceted wisdom and understanding.[12]

Although the similarity of 1:8b with 1:17–18 and Col. 1:9 make a firm decision difficult, it seems best to follow the minority position and understand the phrase as a reference to God’s wisdom. When we look at the epistle from the perspective of those who read it or heard it read for the first time, this argument becomes even more persuasive. Paul’s first audience encountered the phrase in 1:8 without the benefit of knowing that in a moment, in 1:17–18, he would describe his prayer that God might give them wisdom. They also did not know what Paul had told the Colossians in Col. 1:9. It is possible that Paul simply did not think of how the phrase would be understood by those who first heard it read and was already thinking ahead to his prayer report in 1:17–18.﻿[13] It is also possible that he allowed Col. 1:9, which he had recently dictated, to govern the meaning of his language here. In the absence of any firm indication that either of these possibilities played a role in his thinking, however, it seems wise to apply Occam’s razor and interpret the phrase in the simplest way grammatically and stylistically.

Should ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει go with ἐπερίσσευσεν before it or with γνωρίσας after it? Again, the minority position seems to make best sense of the Greek. The parallel between the structure of verse 8 and the structure of verse 6b offers an objective guide for understanding the phrase. In addition, most of the adverbial prepositional phrases in 1:3–14 appear after rather than before the verbs they qualify, and this makes it likely that the phrase goes with ἐπερίσσευσεν, which precedes it, rather than γνωρίσας, which follows it (cf. Hoehner 2002: 213).

If this is correct, then Paul is saying that when God lavished his grace upon his people, it was not a haphazard or ill-considered action. Just as God chose his people before the foundation of the world (v. 4), predetermined that he would adopt them as his children (v. 5a), and did so in joyous agreement with his considered purpose (v. 5b), so also his decision to lavish his grace upon his people by paying the cost of their redemption in the death of his Beloved Son was in accord with his infinite capacity for wisdom and understanding. Once again, Paul emphasizes that God’s graciousness to his people is not a marginal or occasional characteristic of his dealings with his people, but integral to his character and thus to the way he acts.

[1:9–10] Mention of God’s wisdom and understanding provides the transition to another way in which God has lavished his grace on his people. The participle γνωρίσας is dependent on the verb ἐπερίσσευσεν and further describes how God made his grace abound to his people. It does not, therefore, signal a new step in the argument (pace Caragounis 1977: 93; Best 1998: 133). God has also lavished his grace on believers by making known to them τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ (to mystērion tou thelēmatos autou, the mystery of his will). God has now shared with his people the wisdom and understanding that he put to work when he graciously redeemed them through the death of his Beloved Son.

As many commentators from Origen onward have observed, in verse 9 Paul uses the same stylistic pattern that appears in verse 5.[14] Just as in verse 5 God “determined in advance” (προορίσας, proorisas) that he would adopt believers as his children “according to the good pleasure of his will” (κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, kata tēn eudokian tou thelēmatos autou), so here Paul says that he has “made known” (γνωρίσας, gnōrisas) the mystery of his will to his people “according to his good pleasure, which he planned in him” (κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτοῦ ἣν προέθετο ἐν αὐτῷ, kata tēn eudokian autou hēn proetheto en autō). Many commentators observe that the prefix προ- on the verb προέθετο does not normally carry connotations of “prior” planning (cf., e.g., Rom. 1:13; 3:25; 3 Macc. 2:27; e.g., Lightfoot 1895: 318; Lincoln 1990: 31), but since the temporal connotations of the preposition πρό receive such emphasis throughout the benediction (πρό, v. 4; προορίσας, v. 5; προορισθέντες and πρόθεσιν, v. 11; προηλπικότας, v. 12), it seems likely that Paul intended a similar emphasis here (Schlier 1957: 63; Gnilka 1971: 78; cf. Best 1998: 138).[15] In verses 5 and 9b, therefore, Paul links the prior decision of God to his pleasure in accomplishing his will (Cambier 1963: 85). In verse 5 God was pleased to decide in advance to adopt believers as his children. In verse 9b Paul says that when God graciously revealed the mystery of his will to them, he did so in accord with prior plans laid down for his own delight.

As the additional note explains, the term μυστήριον (mystērion, mystery) refers in a general sense to God’s gracious revelation to his people of something they could not possibly know unless he had made it known (cf. Dan. 2:17–30). Paul describes this mystery more fully in verses 9b–10, and he does this in three phrases that qualify the clause γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον (gnōrisas hēmin to mystērion, by making known to us the mystery). His first two qualifying phrases say something about God’s action of making the mystery known to his people, and the third qualifying phrase tells what the mystery is.

The first qualifying phrase explains that God made the mystery known to his people κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτοῦ ἣν προέθετο ἐν αὐτῷ (kata tēn eudokian autou hēn proetheto en autō, according to his good pleasure, which he planned in him). Two aspects of this statement are important for a full understanding of the benediction at this point. First, just as in verse 5 God predestined his people for adoption according to the good pleasure of his will, so here God made the mystery known to them according to plans that he laid for his good pleasure.[16] It is hard to miss the emphasis on the delight that God has taken in laying out his plans, whether to adopt his people as his children or to reveal to them the mystery of his will. Second, God has planned to reveal the mystery to his people ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him), that is, in Christ. Just as their adoption, according to verse 5, took place through Christ, so God’s plans to reveal the mystery to them revolve around Christ.

The second qualifying phrase says that God has revealed the mystery to his people according to plans laid εἰς οἰκονομίαν τοῦ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν (eis oikonomian tou plērōmatos tōn kairōn, for administering the fullness of the times). Although Paul’s grammar is ambiguous here, we should probably understand εἰς (eis) not to mean “at the time of” (Hoehner 2002: 217) or “in reference to” (Eadie 1883: 50; Lightfoot 1895: 319), but “for the purpose of.”[17] We should probably also take οἰκονομίαν (oikonomian, administration) not as a reference to Paul’s role as administrator of God’s mysteries (Eph. 3:2; Col. 1:25–26; cf. 1 Cor. 9:17), or as a reference to God’s plan itself (cf. 3:9), but to God’s work of administering the plan that he decided on according to his good pleasure (cf. Luke 16:2).[18] When Paul says that God has made his plans in Christ for the purpose of administering “the fullness of the times,” he probably has in mind God’s control over the unfolding of successive historical periods, just as in Daniel the God who revealed mysteries (2:19, 22) was the God who “changes times [καιρούς, kairous] and seasons [χρόνους, chronous]” (Dan. 2:21 OG, Theod.).[19]

To summarize, God made the mystery known to his people because it gave him pleasure to do this, and to do it in a way that made Christ of central importance. His revelation of the mystery to his people was part of his administrative work within history for accomplishing his ultimate purposes.

The third qualifying phrase summarizes the content of the mystery and states God’s ultimate purposes. It is not immediately obvious that the phrase ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ (anakephalaiōsasthai ta panta en tō Christō, to sum up all things in Christ) relays the content of the mystery. It is separated from the phrase “the mystery of his will” by two subordinate clauses, the first of which contains a verb (προέθετο, proetheto, planned) whose meaning is often completed with an infinitive.[20] Paul might be saying, therefore, that God planned to sum up all things in Christ rather than that the mystery he revealed to his people was the summing up of all things in Christ.

Despite this ambiguity it is likely that Paul intended for the infinitive to describe the mystery’s content. In a section of the letter designed to praise God for the revelation of the mystery of his will, it would make little sense to leave the reader guessing about the mystery’s content and the goal toward which “the times” were moving. Moreover, Paul uses a similar construction in 3:3–6. There he mentions the mystery twice in verses 3–4 but does not define it more closely until verse 6, and he packages this more-detailed definition in an infinitive construction (εἶναι τὰ ἔθνη . . . , einai ta ethnē . . . , that the Gentiles are . . .) just as he does here in 1:10.

The mystery of God’s will that he has graciously revealed to his people, therefore, is the ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι (anakephalaiōsasthai) of all things in Christ. This is an unusual word in Greek literature, and Paul’s use of it here has led to two exegetical errors, each of which focuses on one element of the word (either ἀνά or κεφαλαιόω) rather than the normal meaning of the term taken as a whole. The first approach focuses on the preposition ἀνά (ana) attached to the beginning of the verb. When compounded with verbs, ἀνά can connote “repetition and improvement” (LSJ 98) in a way similar to the English prefix re-. Jerome, accordingly, thought that ἀνακεφαλαιόω (anakephalaioō) referred to Christ’s repetition and perfection of salvation history in himself (e.g., Jerome [Heine 2002: 97–98]), and both Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.34–35) and John of Damascus (PG 95:824–25) seem to have similarly thought that it referred to the restoration of the fallen creation in the incarnation of Christ (see McHugh 1982: 308). The common use of the term, however, does not emphasize the restoration of what was broken or damaged but the orderly summation of what was previously laid out in piecemeal form.

The second approach argues that Paul, or the author of Ephesians, made a conceptual link between ἀνακεφαλαιόω and the important theme, developed later in the letter, of Christ’s headship over all things and over the church (1:22; 4:15; 5:23). These interpreters are aware that ἀνακεφαλαιόω is formed not from the noun κεφαλή (kephalē), meaning “head,” but from the noun κεφάλαιον (kephalaion), meaning “a brief statement concerning some topic or subject, main thing, main point,” and that its corresponding verb, κεφαλαιόω (kephalaioō) means to “sum up” (BDAG 541). They still think, however, that Paul linked ἀνακεφαλαιόω with the notion of Christ’s headship.[21] If they are correct, then the mystery that God revealed to his people is his plan to “head up all things in Christ.” On this reading, Paul says that God will place Christ as the head over all things.

The trouble with this approach lies in the location of the word in the flow of the letter. This is the first occurrence in the text of any term with the κεφαλ- root, and so Paul has not yet explained his thesis that Christ will be the head over all things or over the church. It is unlikely that he gave the term a special meaning that his readers could determine only from what he wrote later in the letter.

The noun ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (anakephalaiōsis) and its corresponding verb ἀνακεφαλαιόω were commonly used in rhetorical contexts of an orator’s or author’s “recapitulation” or “summary” of the various elements of a speech or composition (LSJ 108; LSJSup 27), and this use of the term provides the most help in understanding Paul’s use of it here. The Roman rhetorical theorist Quintilian, only slightly younger than Paul and also writing in the first century, defined the noun ἀνακεφαλαίωσις as “the repetition and grouping of facts” that should come at the end of a speech in court “both to refresh the memory of the judge and to place the whole case before his eyes.” This device is especially useful, Quintilian says, because although the details of the case may have made little impression on the judge, “their cumulative effect is considerable” (Inst. 6.1.1). For Quintilian, therefore, the noun ἀνακεφαλαίωσις refers to a collection of the essential data of a case into a brief, coherent form that both reminds one of the crucial points scattered throughout the preceding speech and makes the point of the whole argument clear.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, writing at the turn of the first century, could use the term in the same way, this time of the unfolding of his written composition Roman Antiquities. At the end of book 1, he says that he will begin book 2 with the ἀνακεφαλαίωσις of what he has shown in his first book (Ant. rom. 1.90.2), meaning that he will neatly summarize the main points of that section.[22] Paul probably had something similar in mind in the only other use of the word (here too in its verbal form) in the NT. In Rom. 13:9 he says that the Mosaic law’s commandments concerning relationships among people “are summed up” in the sentence “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18).

If Paul used the term in Eph. 1:10 with this common oratorical and literary meaning, then he is metaphorically describing God’s plan to sum up his disparate creation in Christ. Just as an orator or writer draws together the elements of an argument and shows how they demonstrate the chief point of the speech or composition, so Christ will bring order to the universe. God will use Christ to bring together the disparate elements of creation whether they are “things in the heavens” or “things on the earth” (cf. Lightfoot 1895: 321–22).

Later, Paul will explain in detail what he means by this: God will unify the created universe around Christ. Through the resurrection and ascension of Christ, God has conquered all powers inimical to his purposes and placed them, vanquished, at Christ’s feet (1:20–22a). God has given this conquering Christ to his body, the church (1:22b–23), and the church is itself comprised of believers drawn from people groups formerly alienated both from God (2:1–10) and from one another (2:11–22). Christ will therefore be head over all things (1:22), especially the church (4:15; 5:23). This important theme in Ephesians recalls 1 Cor. 15:28 (where all things are subjected to the Son, and the Son to God), Phil. 2:10 (where every creature—heavenly, earthly, and subterranean—pays homage to Jesus for God’s glory), and especially Col. 1:20 (where God reconciles all things, whether in heaven or on earth, to himself through Christ; Masson 1953: 145).

We should not, however, get ahead of Paul at this point in the argument (cf. Lincoln 1990: 33). Here Paul says only that the mystery of God’s will, which he graciously made known to his people, reveals that God intends to sum up in Christ the disparate elements of the universe, both heavenly and earthly. Christ will emerge as the organizing principle of all creation.

Summary

In 1:7–10 Paul praises God for two further blessings he has given to his people. First, he has purchased them out of a metaphorical slavery by forgiving their transgressions against him. This has happened at the high price of the death of his Beloved Son on the cross and was no haphazard plan but in accord with God’s wisdom and understanding. God’s carefully considered willingness to pay such a price for the forgiveness of the sins of his people reveals something about his character: he is not merely a gracious God but an overwhelmingly gracious God. Second, God has blessed his people by revealing to them something they could not have deduced themselves: God is in the process of organizing the entire universe, both its heavenly dimension and its earthly dimension, around Christ. The historical course of the universe finds its organizational principle in him.



Additional Note

1:9–10. The term μυστήριον was used widely in religious contexts where Greek was spoken in antiquity. In Greco-Roman cultural contexts, beginning in the seventh century BC (Heraclitus, frag. 14), it referred to the secret rites of various religions in which initiates were united with a god (Bornkamm, TDNT 4:803; Harvey 1980: 321), and especially to the secret religious rituals practiced at Eleusis (Caragounis 1977: 5–6). This union took place through reenacting various significant events in that god’s existence, such as suffering, death, and rebirth (Bornkamm, TDNT 4:805). These religions placed their adherents under strict codes of secrecy, not about the goal of these rites, which was often a pleasant existence in the afterlife, but about the details of the rituals (Bornkamm, TDNT 4:806–8; Harvey 1980: 321). The term “mystery” also appeared widely in other religious contexts, such as philosophy and magic, as a reference to esoteric knowledge that either resulted from or led to contact with the divine (Bornkamm, TDNT 4:808–13; cf. Harvey 1980: 321–22).

Beginning in the Hellenistic period, Jewish writers used the term in both positive and negative ways. The Wisdom of Solomon, for example, speaks both positively of “the mysteries [μυστήρια] of God” that the wicked do not know (2:22) and negatively of the “mysteries and mystic initiatory rites” that idolatrous pagans practice and hand down from one generation to the next (14:15, 23). Here, “the mysteries of God” seem to refer to the rewards that the righteous will receive in the afterlife (cf. 1 En. 103.2–4; 1 Cor. 2:9; Brown 1968: 10; Winston 1979: 120–21).[23]

Elsewhere in Jewish literature from the Second Temple period, the Greek term, or its equivalent in one of the Semitic languages, can refer to the mysterious rationale that lies beneath God’s ordering and assigning symbolic meaning to cosmic phenomena and bodies such as lightning, thunder, wind, clouds, dew, sun, moon, and stars (1 En. 41.3; 43.1–4; 1QHa 9.11; cf. Brown 1968: 15). Both the actions of evil beings, such as the magical rituals of fallen angels, and the actions of the righteous are “secrets” that God knows (1 En. 9.6–8; 16.3; cf. 1Qap Genar 1.1; 1Q27 frag. 1, col. 1.1; 1QM 14.9; 1QHa 13.36; 4Q429 frag. 1, col. 4.10). Apparently this means that God knows why such rituals operate in the way they do and what motivates the righteous to do good (Brown 1968: 16–17).

The most characteristic use of the term “mystery” in a Jewish context, however, is visible clearly in the Greek text of Daniel, which uses it to translate the Aramaic word רָז (rāz). In this context the term refers to the knowledge of God’s orchestration of the future rise and fall of kingdoms in history, particularly as these events move the universe toward “the last days” (Dan. 2:28–29 LXX; cf. 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 10:38, 59; 2 Bar. 48.3; 54.1; 81.4; 82.2; 83.6–7; 1QS 4.18; 11.3; 1Q27 frag. 1, col. 1.3–4; 1QHa 5.19). This knowledge resides with God, and those who possess it only do so because God has revealed it to them (Dan. 2:18–19, 27–28, 30, 47 LXX; 1QS 10.3). In 2 Baruch, God similarly “made known” to Baruch “the mysteries of the times” and “the coming of the periods” (cf. 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 10:38–59). God reveals these mysteries concerning the unfolding and end of history to Baruch “according to the multitude of his grace” and “the magnitude of his mercy” (2 Bar. 81; OTP 1:649), a point that, although not as explicit, is nevertheless present in Dan. 2, where God mercifully saves the lives of Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego by revealing the “mystery” of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream to them (see esp. Dan. 2:18 MT, Theod.).

Sometimes in these Jewish contexts, the term continues to carry the connotations of esoteric knowledge that it had within the mystery religions, a knowledge available only to certain cognoscenti. In the Old Greek version of Daniel (but in neither the MT nor Theodotion’s version), for example, Daniel “proclaimed a fast and supplication and that help be sought from the Lord Most High about this mystery” of the king’s dream and its interpretation (Dan. 2:18 NETS). After this, the king’s “mystery” is revealed clearly to Daniel in a nighttime vision (2:19). This version of the story leaves the impression that Daniel received the vision because of his exemplary piety. Similarly, in 2 Esdras (4 Ezra), God reveals “many secrets” to Ezra because he has seen his “righteous conduct” (10:38–39; cf. 12:36), and some of Ezra’s visions come to him after he has wept and fasted for seven days (5:20; 6:35; cf. 9:23–28).

The term appears far more often in the Pauline corpus than in other early Christian literature and is especially characteristic of Colossians and Ephesians.[24] In the undisputed Pauline letters μυστήριον can have esoteric connotations, just as in the mystery religions and in some Jewish apocalypses. Paul and his fellow apostles have a special role, vaguely like that of the apocalyptic seers, as “administrators of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4:1). Similarly, Paul knows that those who speak in tongues are not understood apart from an interpretation of their speaking because they speak “mysteries in the Spirit” (1 Cor. 14:2; cf. 2 Cor. 12:4). Those who “have prophecy” can understand “mysteries” (1 Cor. 13:2).

There is no hint, however, that any of these persons, including the apostles, received their special revelation because they were more righteous than others. The opposite seems rather to be the case. Paul defines “administrators of the mysteries of God” as “helpers (ὑπηρέτας) of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:1), emphasizing their subordinate and serving role rather than their lofty status. One can understand “all mysteries” and yet be “nothing” if one’s great knowledge is unaccompanied by love (13:2). Similarly, mysteries spoken in uninterpreted tongues and therefore kept inaccessible to the church are not useful for building up the church and must give way to prophecy, which is intelligible and edifying to everyone (14:1–2). The apostle, tongues speaker, and prophet, therefore, are unusual because they have access to knowledge that is not available to others, not because their piety or ascetic discipline has been rewarded with special revelation.

In the Pauline corpus (excluding, for the moment, Ephesians), the term most often carries the common Jewish connotation of God’s knowledge of the unfolding of events in the last days, a knowledge that would be unavailable to human beings unless God had graciously revealed it to them. Paul can speak of various elements of this unfolding eschatological scenario as mysteries. In 2 Thess. 2:7, μυστήριον describes the increase in evil during the last days; in Rom. 11:25 the eschatological influx of Israelite believers into the people of God; in 1 Cor. 15:51 the transformation of the bodies of believers who are alive when the last trumpet sounds and God raises the dead; and in Col. 1:27 (cf. Rom. 16:25–26) the inclusion of the Gentiles within the people of God. The most characteristic use of the term in the Pauline corpus, however, describes the gospel and Christ, who stands at its center, as eschatological events that have happened according to God’s historically enacted plan for salvation (1 Cor. 2:1–2; 4:1; Col. 1:27; 2:2; 4:3; 1 Tim. 3:16; cf. 3:9).[25] God had predetermined the crucifixion of Christ before the ages for the purpose of “our glory” (1 Cor. 2:7; Col. 1:27), but this μυστήριον remained hidden until God revealed it to the saints (1 Cor. 2:7; Rom. 16:25; Col. 1:26). Paul and the other apostles are “administrators” of these “mysteries” (1 Cor. 4:1; Col. 1:25–26; 4:3).

In Ephesians, Paul’s use of the term falls in step with these other occurrences. Paul can use μυστήριον in its most fundamental sense as a way to describe the gospel (6:19) or Christ (3:4), hidden until God revealed them (3:9). Just as in the undisputed letters and in Colossians, God has given to Paul and other apostles and prophets the responsibility of administering this gospel mystery by telling others about it (3:2–5; 6:19; cf. Col. 1:25–27).[26] As with the other letters, however, Paul’s piety or ascetic heroism did not win him this role. To the contrary, he is the least of all the saints, but God has graciously given him the task of illuminating others about the mystery (Eph. 3:2, 7–9).[27]

Just as in the other letters, the union of all peoples—Gentiles and Jews—in one eschatologically restored people is a mystery (Eph. 3:4, 6; Rom. 11:25; 16:25–26; Col. 1:27), but in Ephesians this element of the mystery rises to prominence. Paul defines “the mystery of Christ” as the union of Jewish and Gentile believers together in one body (Eph. 3:3, 6; cf. 2:16), and defines the unified body, in turn, both as the church (3:10; cf. 1:23) and as the body of Christ (4:12–13; 5:23, 30). In 5:32, therefore, Paul reveals to his readers the “great mystery” that Gen. 2:24 refers not merely to the union of husband and wife but also to the union of Christ with the church.

Here in 1:9, μυστήριον refers to the knowledge that God intends to sum up all things in Christ. The revelation of this mystery is a blessing: it is one of the ways in which God lavishly pours out his grace on believers (cf. Dan. 2:17–30). The content of the mystery is that God is unifying the cosmos, whether earthly or heavenly, in Christ. Because the church is comprised of both Gentiles and Jews (Eph. 2:11–22; 3:4–7) and as a united entity forms the body of Christ (4:13, 16), it plays a critical role in the outworking of this mystery.





II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)


C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

The turning point from the second to the third section of the benediction repeats the structure of the turning point from the first to the second section. Just as the phrase “in the Beloved, in whom” (vv. 6b–7a) provided the bridge for crossing from the first to the second section, so the phrase “in him, in whom” (vv. 10b–11a) provides the bridge for crossing from the second to the third section.

This third section returns to the themes of the first section. The idea that God chose his people because he predetermined them for adoption in verses 4–5 reappears in the statement that God made them his heirs because he predetermined them in verse 11. Just as the notions of God’s choice and adoption of his people in verses 4–5 recall the biblical emphasis on Israel as God’s people, so the notion that God’s people are his heirs is redolent of the biblical theme of Israel as the children, and therefore heirs, of God. Similarly, just as Paul uses a prepositional phrase in verse 5 to emphasize the deliberate nature of God’s decision to choose his people and adopt them (“according to the good pleasure of his will”), so Paul uses two prepositional phrases in verse 11 to underline the thoughtful and deliberate nature of God’s decision to make them his heirs (“according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will”). Finally, just as the first section of the benediction ends with an expression of the purpose behind God’s decision to adopt believers as his people (“for the praise of his glorious grace”), followed by a brief tag (“which he gave us in the Beloved”), so verse 12 ends with the same expression of purpose (“that we might exist for the praise of his glory”), followed by a brief phrase (“we who hope beforehand in Christ”).

Although this third section recalls the major themes of the first section, it also advances the thought of the benediction. Paul takes the thought that believers are God’s chosen people and adopted children a step further than he had in verses 4–5: as God’s children they are also his heirs (v. 11; cf. Rom. 8:17). In verse 11 Paul also places even greater emphasis on the deliberate nature of God’s action of making believers his heirs: God did not simply predetermine that they would be his children because it gave him pleasure to do so (v. 5), but in his capacity as the God who effects all things, he also worked very deliberately to make believers his heirs; he did this in accord with his “purpose” and the “counsel” that resulted in the doing of his “will.”

Perhaps most important, Paul ends the third section by briefly describing the eschatological tension in which all believers live. The benediction’s second section (vv. 7–10) has spoken of God’s plan “to sum up all things in Christ, things in the heavens and things on the earth in him” (v. 10). Christ is the very person in whom all Christians exist, and therefore the participation of all believers in this summing up of all things is assured. Now, however, before all that happens, believers live in hope that it will happen, a hope that is not some fragile expectation that may or may not come to pass, but a hope whose basis is Christ himself. God has made his people heirs so that even now “we who hope beforehand”—before the full summation of all things in Christ—will exist for the praise of his glory.



Exegesis and Exposition

11. . . in whom also we have been made heirs, because we were predestined according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will 12in order that we might exist for the praise of his glory—we who hope beforehand in Christ, . . .

[1:11] Paul begins the third section of the benediction with the claim that in Christ—the Christ in whom God will sum up all things (v. 10)—“we have been made heirs” (ἐκληρώθημεν, eklērōthēmen).
