The verb κληρόω (klēroō) is infrequent in Biblical Greek (appearing only here and in 1 Sam. 14:41 and Isa. 17:11 [2x]), but common in ancient Greek literature generally, where it meant “appoint by lot,” “cast lots,” and by extension, “allot, assign.” In the passive voice it means “appointed by lot” and “allotted” (LSJ 960). If the term carries these normal connotations here, then we should translate it “we have been allotted.”[1] By itself, however, this expression requires some additional information to complete its meaning. What have believers been allotted? Or alternatively, to whom have they been allotted?

Interpreters have often filled in this information from the use of the term in ancient Jewish and Christian texts. In the OT, sometimes Israel or its various tribes are allotted the land, or portions of it, by God (Num. 26:55–56). At other times, Israel is called God’s allotted portion (Deut. 4:20; 9:29; 32:9; Add. Esth. 13:8–14:19). Some Jewish texts of the Second Temple period speak of those who have a “lot” among God’s people (e.g., Wis. 5:5; 1QS 11.7–8; 1QHa 11.22–23), and this idea reappears not only in Acts 26:18 but also, significantly, in Col. 1:12. If this approach is correct, then Paul could be saying that Christians have been assigned a destiny, or lot, by God. This thought is close to Col. 1:11–12, although there the noun κλῆρος (klēros) rather than the verb κληρόω appears (Abbott 1897: 20; Lincoln 1990: 36). Alternatively, Paul might be saying that either Jewish Christians (O’Brien 1999: 115–16) or Christians generally (Robinson 1904: 34, 146; Alford 1857: 75; Westcott 1906: 14–15) have been allotted to God as his portion, just as Israel of old once filled that role. These approaches to the term have two advantages. First, they are consistent with the common use of the verb κληρόω to mean “allot,” and second, they recognize the probable conceptual connection between Col. 1:12 and Eph. 1:11.

Still, another approach is probably best. Although the verb κληρόω does not mean “inherit,” it shares a root with the nouns κληρονόμος (klēronomos, heir) and κληρονομία (klēronomia, inheritance), and with the verbs κληρονομέω (klēronomeō, inherit) and κατακληρονομέω (kataklēronomeō, inherit). These terms appear throughout the Greek Scriptures in reference to God’s people as his “heirs” (Rom. 8:17; cf. James 2:5), to the land as Israel’s “inheritance” or as something they will “inherit” (Num. 33:54; Deut. 4:1; Acts 13:19; cf. Zech. 8:12), and to God’s people as God’s “inheritance” (Deut. 32:9) or as something he will “inherit” (Zech. 2:16 [ 2:12 MT, Eng.]). Sometimes, the verbal idea that Israel “will inherit” (κατακληρονομήσετε, kataklēronomēsete) the land is linked with the notion that God will give the land to Israel “by lot” (ἐν κλήρῳ, en klērō; Num. 33:53–54; 34:13). This is probably the concept that stands behind Col. 1:12, which speaks of God qualifying Christians to have a “portion of the lot of the saints in light” (τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ φωτί, tēn merida tou klērou tōn hagiōn en tō phōti; Dunn 1996: 75–76).

In the Ephesians benediction itself, Paul will say in verse 14 that the Spirit is “the down payment of our inheritance” (κληρονομίας ἡμῶν, klēronomias hēmōn), a phrase that, as we will see below, refers to the eschatological inheritance of God’s kingdom, over which Jesus, the Messiah, rules as God’s vice regent (5:5). In verse 18 Paul will speak of God’s “inheritance in the saints” (τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις, tēs klēronomias autou en tois hagiois). It seems probable, therefore, that when Paul uses the term ἐκληρώθημεν here in verse 11, he intends for it to refer not simply to an “allotment” or “portion” that has been given either to believers or to God, but specifically to an “inheritance” that has been given either to believers or to God.

But is the inheritance theirs or God’s? Since Paul will speak of the inheritance of believers in the next subsection of the benediction (v. 14), it seems likely that he also intends to refer here to the status of believers as heirs. If so, then the thought is similar to that of Rom. 8:17, where Paul describes believers as adopted children of God and therefore his “heirs” (κληρονόμοι, klēronomoi; cf. Gal. 3:29; 4:1, 5, 7).[2] Paul has already praised God for his adoption of believers (Eph. 1:5). Here in 1:11, he praises God for making believers his heirs.

Paul next says that this blessing came to God’s people “because we were predestined” (προορισθέντες, prooristhentes) to have it. The thought here is similar to that of verse 5, where Paul uses the same term, although in the active rather than the passive voice (προορίσας, proorisas). Just as in verse 5 God has chosen believers because he has predestined them for adoption, so here God has made them his heirs because he has predestined them. Moreover, just as in verse 5 Paul says that God has predestined believers for adoption “according to the good pleasure of his will,” so here he says that believers were predestined “according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will.” In both places his basic thought is the same: the blessing of God’s relationship with his people comes at God’s joyfully considered initiative. In verse 5, however, the accent falls on the pleasure that God took in his plan for his people. Here the accent falls on the considered nature of that plan. Words that emphasize God’s meticulous planning and sovereign control pile up one upon another: πρόθεσις (prothesis, purpose), ἐνεργέω (energeō, work), βουλή (boulē, counsel), θέλημα (thelēma, will).[3] This piling up of words arises not merely from stylistic verbosity but also from Paul’s desire to encourage his readers to think of themselves as an especially privileged people—privileged not because of their accomplishments (2:5, 8) but because of what God, who effects all things, has done for them. He carefully planned to make his people his heirs before he did it. This action was neither haphazard nor dependent on anything they would do to earn it.

[1:12] Just as near the end of the first section of the benediction (vv. 4–6) Paul says that God has predestined us to be his adopted children “for the praise of his glorious grace” (v. 6a), so here, near the end of the third section, Paul says that believers were made heirs of God “in order that we might exist for the praise of his glory” (v. 12a).

This expression of purpose is so climactic that the phrase added to it almost seems out of place: τοὺς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ (tous proēlpikotas en tō christō, we who hope beforehand in Christ). Here too, however, Paul follows the pattern of verses 5–6, where he adds to the concept that his readers were predestined to praise God’s grace (v. 5–6a) the further thought that God has granted them his grace in the Beloved (v. 6b).

Through the centuries many interpreters have thought that the participle προηλπικότας (proēlpikotas, hope beforehand) referred to Jews who hoped beforehand in the Messiah or, more commonly, to Jewish Christians who, like Paul, were the first to hear the gospel.[4] Paul would then be contrasting “we [Jews] who hoped beforehand in Christ” or even “we [Jews] who hoped beforehand in the Messiah” with the Gentile audience of Ephesians, to whom he refers in verse 13 with the phrase “in whom you also. . . .”

The emergence in 2:11–3:13 of the unity of Gentile Christians and Jewish Christians as an important theme in the letter, and specifically as an important element in the mystery that God has revealed to believers (1:9; cf. 3:3–6), makes this an attractive approach to this final phrase in verse 12. If this approach is correct, then in 1:12–13 Paul anticipates his fuller exposition of that theme later in the letter (Aletti 2001: 79).

This understanding of προηλπικότας, however, is probably incorrect. Up to this point in the benediction, Paul has used the first-person plural (“we”) ten times to refer to all Christians as recipients of the blessings he is describing. It is unlikely that he would expect the first hearers of this letter to understand the first-person-plural subject of προηλπικότας in verse 12b in any other way.[5] It is difficult to see how they could have done so. The phrase ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἐκληρώθημεν (en hō kai eklērōthēmen, in whom also we have been made heirs) at the beginning of the third major section of the benediction (v. 11) is structurally almost identical to the phrase ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν (en hō echomen, in whom we have) at the beginning of second major section (v. 7), and these two phrases contain the only first-person-plural indicative verbs in the entire benediction. Paul would have introduced considerable confusion into the benediction if he meant the “we” of these two verbs to refer to different groups: all Christians in verse 7, and Jews or Jewish Christians in verse 11. Since the “we” of verse 7 must refer to all who have experienced redemption through the blood of God’s Beloved Son, the “we” of verse 11 must likewise refer to all Christians. Similarly, the appearance of a participial form of προορίζω (proorizō, predestine) in both verse 5 and verse 11 makes it unlikely that the first-person-plural subjects of these two participles refer to different groups, yet this would be required if we took προηλπικότας in verse 12b as a reference to Jews only.[6]

What then does προηλπικότας mean? The verb is rare, appearing only here in the NT, never in the LXX, and seldom in ancient Greek literature generally. Where it occurs, it seems to mean “hope for before,” “anticipate,” “expect” (LSJ 1477).[7] Its perfect tense places the reader close to the verb’s action and, in this context, emphasizes the state in which believers live (Campbell 2008b: 24–29; 2008a: 46–52, 103–4, 106–7).[8] The word and its tense-form, then, refers to the expectation that all Christians have for the time when “all things, . . . things in the heavens and things on the earth,” will be fully summed up “in him” (v. 10). The prefixed preposition πρό refers not to the past but to the present time, “before” the consummation takes place, a time in which Christian existence is characterized by hope (cf. 2:12; Haupt 1902a: 27; Masson 1953: 146, pace Lindemann 1975: 100–101; Aletti 2001: 78).[9]

Summary

In this third section of the benediction, Paul praises God because he has made his adopted children his heirs. In other words, they have all the blessings that come with membership in God’s household. Their status as God’s heirs is not a result of some accident or of anything they did but because God carefully planned in advance to give them this blessing. He did this so that his people might exist to praise him not only in the future but also in the present as they wait in hope for all things to take their assigned place in relationship to Christ.





II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)


D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)

The fourth and final section of the benediction turns directly to Paul’s readers to remind them of their conversion and especially of the gift of the Holy Spirit that God gave to them at that time. When they heard and believed the gospel, Paul says, God sealed them by means of the Holy Spirit.

He did this for two reasons. First, the Holy Spirit’s seal protects them from the wrath that God will one day pour out on the wicked. Although Paul does not say this explicitly, it is implied in his use of such words as σωτηρία (sōtēria, salvation), σφραγίζω (sphragizō, seal), and περιποίησις (peripoiēsis, saved remnant). In the context of Paul’s theology and of the Scriptures that Paul used, these terms speak of protection from the destruction that will come to the wicked on the final day when God judges all people. Second, and more positively, the gift of the Holy Spirit also serves as a down payment on the inheritance that he will give to the remnant he has saved from his wrath. The Spirit’s presence with them is a guarantee that when God brings his purposes to an end, he will fully apply to them the redemption that Christ’s death has accomplished for them (v. 7).

As with all the other blessings for which Paul praises God in the benediction, these blessings are applied to the believer “in Christ” (v. 13 [2x]; cf. vv. 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 [2x], 11, 12). Paul’s readers have heard the gospel of salvation, have believed it, and have been sealed by the Holy Spirit in the sphere of reality that Christ defines. The ultimate purpose for these blessings, moreover, is also identical to the ultimate purpose of the others: God has blessed Paul’s readers in this way so that he might receive their praise (v. 14; cf. vv. 6, 12).

The fourth part of the benediction brings the prayer full circle and therefore to a fitting close. Just as the benediction has begun on a note of praise to God for spiritual blessings, so it concludes with a reference to the way God has used the Spirit to bless Paul’s readers along with all Christians, and with an expression of praise to God for this spiritual blessing.



Exegesis and Exposition

13a. . . in whom you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation . . . , 13bin whom you also, when you believed, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, 14⌜who⌝ is the down payment of our inheritance, for the redemption of the ⌜saved remnant⌝, for the praise of his glory.

[1:13a] Paul begins the fourth and final section of the benediction with the phrase ἐν ᾧ (en hō, in whom). This phrase repeats the substance of the ἐν (en, in) phrase before it, just as it did in the “hinges” between the first and second section (v. 6b–7a) and the second and third section (vv. 10b–11a).

Paul follows this phrase with a direct reference to his readers for the first time since the greeting in verse 2: “In whom you also . . .” Although his readers were born Gentiles (2:11–12), as we have seen above, Paul probably did not have the contrast between his own Jewishness and their ethnic origins in mind when he turned to them directly in this verse. He is not saying that just as “we Jews” have been made heirs (v. 12), so “you Gentiles” have been sealed by the promised Holy Spirit (v. 13). Rather, he turns directly to his readers in the final section of the benediction to emphasize that the blessings God has given to all Christians, and that Paul has recounted in verses 4–12, belong to them. The sudden appearance of the second-person pronoun is a way of speaking directly to them and urges them to think of “every spiritual blessing” that Paul has described in the previous verses as not merely the possession of all Christians but also as theirs personally.

If we may take 3:13 as a hint that Paul’s readers were discouraged, then this shift to a personal address at the end of the benediction may signal the purpose behind this opening prayer of praise. Paul designed it to move his readers’ focus away from the potentially discouraging circumstances that plagued both Paul and them and point them instead to the blessings that God has given them in Christ.

The inclusion of his readers “in Christ”—in the sphere in which the blessings he has just described become operative—happened when his readers heard the gospel, believed it, and received God’s eschatological seal of the Holy Spirit. The syntax of the phrase that expresses this thought is difficult because it begins with two adverbial clauses that are not joined together by any connecting word. The two clauses, moreover, begin in the same way, almost as if Paul had dictated the first clause and then suddenly started over again with the second clause before completing the phrase with the main verb:



First adverbial clause: in whom you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation,

Second adverbial clause: in whom you also, when you believed,

Main verb: were sealed. . . .

We should probably not try to repair the broken syntax by supplying some verb in the first clause that could then transform it into a complete sentence with a pattern similar to the second clause.[1] This is simply a broken sentence, or anacoluthon, a common occurrence in the Pauline corpus.[2] Paul began dictating the sentence (“in whom you also, when you heard the word of truth . . .”) and then qualified what he had written with a statement that interrupted the main train of thought (“. . . the gospel of your salvation . . .”). He then started over using a slightly different phrase (“in whom you also, when you believed, . . .”).

This way of taking the syntax clarifies the meaning of the sentence. Both ἀκούσαντες (akousantes, when you heard) and πιστεύσαντες (pisteusantes, when you believed) are adverbial participles of time. Because they are in the aorist tense, we might at first think that they speak of events that occurred prior to the time of the main verb ἐσφραγίσθητε (esphragisthēte, you were sealed), and because the two participles occur one after the other we might think that Paul speaks of a series of events here: his readers heard the gospel, believed it, and then were sealed by the Holy Spirit. If we understand that the sentence is an anacoluthon, however, and that Paul restates the first adverbial clause when he starts the sentence over in the second adverbial clause, then we can see that the two clauses refer not to two different events but to two aspects of the same event: Paul’s readers heard the gospel and believed it at the same time. Moreover, since aorist adverbial participles often describe events that happen at the same time as the main verb when that verb is itself in the aorist tense (Wallace 1996: 624–25), Paul probably conceived of all three events as happening at the same time: hearing the gospel, believing it, and receiving the seal of the Holy Spirit all happened at once.

Taking the sentence as an anacoluthon also helps us to see that the phrase ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες is not trying to say that Christ was the object of his readers’ faith when they believed the gospel (as true as that is). Since the two phrases are set up in a virtually identical way syntactically, the phrase ἐν ᾧ in the second phrase must refer to the sphere in which Paul’s readers believed, just as in the previous clause ἐν ᾧ refers to the sphere in which they heard the gospel. They both heard and believed the gospel “in Christ”—just as every blessing in the benediction comes to Christians “in Christ.”

Paul describes the gospel that his readers heard as both τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας (ton logon tēs alētheias, the word of truth) and as τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας (to euangelion tēs sōtērias, the gospel of salvation). When he attaches the gospel to the concept of truth elsewhere in his letters, he most often intends to draw a contrast between the true version of the gospel and a false version that is competing with it (Gal. 2:5, 14; cf. 2 Cor. 4:2; 2 Tim. 2:15). Such a contrast may have been in the back of his mind when he dictated these words, especially if he had recently written Colossians. That letter was designed to refute a specious philosophy that had melded its teaching with the Christian gospel (Col. 2:3, 8), and there Paul had also described the Colossian Christians’ conversion as a result of hearing τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (tō logō tēs alētheias tou euangeliou, the word of truth, the gospel; Col. 1:5; cf. Eph. 4:14–15).

The gospel that Paul’s readers heard not only was the true gospel, but it also brought σωτηρία (sōtēria, salvation). Some commentators believe that this is the salvation that believers have already received and that is described more fully in 2:1–10. They then contrast this idea of a completed salvation with salvation in the undisputed Pauline letters, where its ongoing (1 Cor. 1:18; 15:2; 2 Cor. 2:15) and future (1 Thess. 5:8–9; 1 Cor. 3:15; 5:5; Phil. 1:19, 28; 2:12; Rom. 5:9–10; 10:9; 11:26; 13:11) aspects predominate (Muddiman 2001: 78–79; cf. Mitton 1973: 59; Lindemann 1975: 102).[3]

It is not at all clear, however, that Paul intends the phrase τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ὑμῶν (to euangelion tēs sōtērias hymōn) to mean “the gospel of your present salvation.” Paul has just said in verse 12 that all Christians live in the hope of God’s final summation of all things in Christ, and in verse 14 he is about to speak of “our inheritance” and of “the redemption” that await Christians in the future. This makes it likely, therefore, that when he says that his readers have heard and believed “the gospel of salvation,” he was thinking of salvation as something for which believers hope and to which they are appointed (cf. 1 Thess. 5:8–9).

[13b–14] When his readers heard and believed the gospel, Paul continues, they were “sealed” with the promised Holy Spirit, who is a “down payment” of believers’ eschatological inheritance. Paul has already mentioned the Spirit in passing in verse 3, when he spoke of the “spiritual blessings” with which God blessed believers “in the heavenly places in Christ.” There he was referring to the blessings he was about to describe in the benediction and implying that they are gifts of the Holy Spirit (Aletti 2001: 56). The gifts themselves, however, rather than their origin with the Spirit, were his main concern there. Now Paul highlights the work of the Spirit much as he has emphasized the work of the Father in verses 4–6 and the work of the Son in verses 7–12 (cf. Cambier 1963: 96).

Paul refers to four aspects of the Spirit’s work in verses 13b–14. First, Paul says that his readers, when they believed, “were sealed with the . . . Holy Spirit, who is the down payment of our inheritance” (ἐσφραγίσθητε τῷ πνεύματι . . . τῷ ἁγίῳ, ὅ ἐστιν ἀρραβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν, esphragisthēte tō pneumati . . . tō hagiō, ho estin arrabōn tēs klēronomias hēmōn). Seals were widely used in Near Eastern antiquity to guarantee the quality, authenticity, or ownership of a piece of property or a legal document. On property, they often gave protection by preventing tampering, and on legal documents, such as a king’s edict, a bill of sale, or a marriage contract, the seals of the interested parties provided evidence against forgery (Fitzer, TDNT 7:943–48).[4] Authenticity seems to be uppermost in Paul’s mind when he uses the image in 2 Cor. 1:22, and he follows it, as here, with a reference to God’s Spirit in the hearts of Paul and his coworkers as a “down payment” (ἀρραβών, arrabōn). The presence of God’s Spirit with them, Paul says, authenticates his ministry among the Corinthians in the face of charges (probably originating with Paul’s opponents) that the fluctuations in his travel plans proved he was vacillating and unreliable (2 Cor. 1:12–21; cf. 1 Cor. 9:2).

Here in Ephesians, however, the thought is slightly different. If we allow Paul’s other use of the sealing metaphor in Ephesians to guide us to the proper meaning here, then it seems to have a stronger orientation toward the future. In Eph. 4:30 Paul speaks of the Holy Spirit as a seal on believers “for the day of redemption” (εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως, eis hēmeran apolytrōseōs). The idea of marking or sealing certain people for future salvation from the wrath that God will bring upon the wicked appears elsewhere in Jewish literature of Paul’s time (Ezek. 9:4; Pss. Sol. 15.6; 2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 6:5; Rev. 7:3–8).[5] This is probably the meaning of the imagery in Eph. 4:30, and if so, then it is probably its meaning here in 1:13–14, where Paul also speaks of future “redemption” (εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν, eis apolytrōsin, v. 14). God has chosen his people from among all humanity, who are “by nature children of wrath” (2:3), and set the seal of his Spirit on them to protect them from the wrath that is coming (5:6).

Second, Paul says that the Spirit’s presence with believers is not only God’s seal on them but also his ἀρραβών, or “down payment,” of the “inheritance” of their salvation that awaits them in the future. When Paul wrote Ephesians, ἀρραβών was a term used in Greek legal custom for an amount of money that someone who wanted a service performed paid to the person who would provide the services (Kerr 1988: 92–93). It was an amount smaller than the total cost of the service and functioned as a guarantee that the full amount would be paid once the service was rendered. Accepting the ἀρραβών also served as commitment from the service provider that he or she would follow through on the contract.[6]

Paul had the blessings that God had given and would give to the believer in view in the benediction, and so it is probably the obligation of the person who paid the ἀρραβών that he has in mind when he uses the metaphor here.[7] God has given believers the Holy Spirit, therefore, as a sign that he will fulfill his commitment to his people in the future and give them their inheritance. Just as the seal of the Spirit marks God’s people for future redemption, so the “down payment” of the Spirit is a sign that God’s promise of redemption is reliable. Here the thought is similar to 2 Cor. 5:5, where Paul says that the presence of the Spirit with him and his coworkers is a guarantee that God will one day replace their mortal existence with immortality.

The ἀρραβών metaphor, therefore, is the positive counterpart to the sealing metaphor. The Spirit’s sealing function assures believers they will be redeemed rather than destroyed on the day of God’s wrath. The Spirit’s function as a “down payment” assures them of redemption in the future and of the greatness of that redemption in comparison to the present.

Third, believers have been sealed by the Spirit in Christ (ἐν ᾧ, en hō, in whom). Their relationship with Christ is the sphere in which the blessing of the Spirit has come to them. Even here where Paul highlights the Spirit’s work, therefore, the centrality of Christ is also prominent. God’s people experience the eschatological gift of the Spirit only insofar as they have heard and believed the gospel that redemption from sin comes through the sacrificial death of Jesus (v. 7).

Fourth, the Spirit is τῷ πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ (tō pneumati tēs epangelias tō hagiō), “the promised Holy Spirit,” taking the genitive τῆς ἐπαγγελίας as a genitive of quality (BDF §165; Wallace 1996: 86–88). Here Paul speaks of the fulfillment of the prophetic promise that in the days of Israel’s eschatological restoration, God’s Spirit would dwell among his people (Isa. 32:15; 44:3; Ezek. 11:19; 36:26–27; 37:14; Joel 3:1–2 [2:28–29 Eng.]; cf. Gal. 3:14; Acts 1:4; 2:33).[8] This fulfillment has happened “in Christ.”

Paul finishes this section of the benediction with the statement that his readers have heard and believed the gospel and have been sealed by the Holy Spirit εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως (eis apolytrōsin tēs peripoiēseōs, for the redemption of the saved remnant). Ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis) refers not to the redemption that Christ accomplished through his blood, as it did in verse 7, but to the completion of that redemption in the future. This shift from the past to the future is evident from the connection of redemption here to the metaphor of a “down payment.” The “redemption” of believers is metaphorically the full amount of which the Spirit is the “down payment,” and so, at this point in the benediction, our “redemption” must lie in the future (cf. 4:30).

God will bring redemption, Paul says, to the περιποίησις (peripoiēsis), a term whose meaning is difficult to determine. Most commentators opt to see it as a reference either to God’s people as his “possession” or to the “acquisition” of salvation by God’s people. The thought would then move in either of two directions, depending on the translation that one chooses. If we choose “possession,” then God has given the Holy Spirit as a down payment on the inheritance that believers will receive, and he has done this for the purpose of (or until) the redemption of his own possession. Since the noun περιποίησις has no qualifier to tell us whose possession it is, this reading assumes that the possession is God’s and that it refers to God’s people as his special possession.

If we choose “acquisition,” then God gave the Spirit as the down payment on the eschatological inheritance of God’s people until the full redemption, and this redemption is his people’s acquisition of the inheritance. This second reading requires that we understand the genitive τῆς περιποιήσεως as an epexegetical genitive—a genitive-case noun that further explains the noun it qualifies—and that we complete its meaning mentally with some such noun as “inheritance” or “salvation” (Schnackenburg 1991: 45, 67; Best 1998: 153).

As I argue in the additional note, however, the common meaning “the saved remnant” for ἡ περιποίησις fits the context here well and is probably the way Paul meant for his readers to understand the term (Bengel 1860: 4.69; LSJ 1384). On this reading, there is no need to supply anything to complete the meaning of the term. Paul simply says that God gave the Holy Spirit to believers in order to seal them against destruction on the final day and for the purpose of redeeming the remnant whom he will graciously save on that day.

In verses 13–14, therefore, Paul says that God has sealed his readers with the promised Holy Spirit for two reasons. First, he has done this to provide them with a down payment on their future inheritance—tangible assurance that they are part of his people whom he will save. Second, he has done this so that they might be redeemed from the outpouring of his wrath on the final day.

Paul concludes not only this fourth section of the benediction, but also the benediction itself, by stating the ultimate purpose for which God has sealed Christians with the Holy Spirit and intends to redeem and save them in the future. He has done this εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ (eis epainon tēs doxēs autou, for the praise of his glory). This statement recalls the benediction’s opening expression of praise: “Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us . . .” (v. 3). It also recalls the expressions of praise that punctuate the benediction at the conclusions of the first and third subsections. God has predetermined that he will adopt his people as his children through Jesus Christ “for the praise of his glorious grace” (v. 6), and he has predetermined that he will make them his heirs in Christ so that they may exist “for the praise of his glory” (v. 12). This concluding doxology therefore describes not only why God intended to redeem those whom he has sealed in Christ with the Holy Spirit (vv. 13–14) but also why he “blessed [them] with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (v. 3). He did all this “for the praise of his glory.”

Summary

In this final part of the benediction, Paul addresses his readers directly to emphasize that all the blessings that come to those who are in Christ, and that he has described in verses 3–12, also belong to them. This happened when they heard the gospel, believed the gospel, and entered the sphere of existence defined by Christ. In that place, the Holy Spirit began his work in their lives. The Holy Spirit sealed Paul’s readers, keeping them safe from God’s eschatological wrath, and provided them with a guarantee of the inheritance that God has promised to his people. God did all this in order that Paul’s readers, as members of God’s people, might praise him. Paul has provided a model for this sort of praise in his benedictory prayer.



Additional Notes

1:14. Instead of ὅ (which appears in 𝔓46, A, B, F, G, L, P, 6, 81, 104, 365, 1175, 1505, 1739, 1881 [among others], two Old Latin manuscripts, the Syriac Peshitta, and the Latin version of Irenaeus), a number of manuscripts have the nominative masculine relative pronoun ὅς (א, D, Ψ, 33, 𝔐). It is very difficult to decide between the two readings on both the evidence of these witnesses and the stylistic probabilities. The differences in modern editions and commentators reveal the difficulty of the problem. Among the editions, Tischendorf, Westcott and Hort’s margin, Vogels, Merk, and NA25 all opt for ὅς, and among commentators Hoehner argues cautiously for the same reading on the basis of slightly superior manuscript evidence. The evidence for ὅς, he says, has a marginally better geographical distribution than the evidence for ὅ (Hoehner 2002: 241). Metzger (1994: 533) and NA27 conclude, to the contrary, that the manuscript evidence points toward the originality of ὅ.

Grammatically, either reading works equally well: the neuter relative pronoun agrees in gender with its neuter antecedent πνεύματι, and the masculine relative pronoun agrees in gender with the predicate nominative ἀρραβών. A firm decision is virtually impossible yet also does not affect the meaning of the passage. Since the issue is one simply of grammatical gender, the question of whether the Holy Spirit is a person or a force does not come into play (Wallace 1996: 338). Clearly, if the Holy Spirit can be grieved (4:30), he is a person.

1:14. The term περιποίησις is a “noun of action,” derived from the verb περιποιέω, which can mean “preserve,” “save up,” “obtain,” or “procure” in the active voice, and in the middle voice can mean “keep or save for oneself,” “acquire.” This verb has the meaning “save for oneself” in Luke 17:33 and “acquire” in Acts 20:28 and 1 Tim. 3:13.[9] The noun, by analogy, means “preservation” or “acquisition” (LSJ 1384); when it means “acquisition,” it can refer to the act of acquiring something, or to that which is acquired, or when the action of acquiring falls into the background, simply to a “possession.” The range of meanings appears in the LXX and in the NT—“preservation” (or “remnant”) in 2 Chron. 14:12 (LXX, MT, 14:13 Eng.) and Heb. 10:39; “the act of acquiring” in 2 Thess. 2:14; “a thing acquired” in Hag. 2:9; and possibly, although this is debatable, a “possession” in Mal. 3:17.

Virtually all modern interpreters of Eph. 1:14 discuss the word here as if only two options for understanding it are available.[10] One group believes that the word has the sense of “a thing acquired,” a “possession,” and that Paul uses it to refer to God’s people. They are his “possession,” as in Exod. 19:5 (cf. 23:22 LXX), and Paul speaks here of God’s eventual redemption of that possession. Often these interpreters point to 1 Pet. 2:9, where the term appears in an allusion to Mal. 3:17 LXX. These interpreters assume that in Mal. 3:17 περιποίησις means “possession.”[11]

Unfortunately, in Exod. 19:5 LXX the term is περιούσιος rather than περιποίησις, and as opponents of this view are fond of pointing out, if περιποίησις in Mal. 3:17 and 1 Pet. 2:9 refers to God’s possession, it does so not because of any technical meaning for the word as “God’s special people” but because the broader context in both cases makes clear that God’s people are his “possession.” In Eph. 1:14, say these interpreters, there is no word such as αὐτοῦ that makes the term refer specifically to God’s possession.[12] This leaves only the meaning “acquisition” for the term. Paul, then, speaks of “the redemption of the acquisition,” and the term refers to “that full and final achievement of salvation, to which the addressees are called through the ‘gospel of salvation’ and in which they have already received a share” (Schnackenburg 1991: 67).[13] Both ways of understanding περιποίησις assume that Paul (or the author) has expressed himself ambiguously and left his readers to figure out the basic point of the phrase.

It is curious that the common meaning “something preserved” has received so little attention among interpreters. In the eighteenth century, John Albert Bengel (1860: 4.69) read it this way: “Περιποίησις is said of that which remains still, when all other things perish.” In modern times, the classical Greek lexicon LSJ also chose this meaning, translating περιποίησις here as “those who are saved” (LSJ 1384). To my knowledge, no other interpreter of Ephesians has read the word in this way.

Despite its rare appearance in the interpretive literature on Ephesians, however, this meaning represents a natural understanding of the term both within the wider context of Greek usage and within the narrower context of Ephesians. Where it appears in Greek literature generally, including the Greek Scriptures, the term frequently refers to the preservation of a remnant in the context of war or some other hardship. The pseudo-Platonic Definitions treats the term in the course of discussing words connected with war. “Salvation,” it says, “is preservation without harm” (σωτηρία περιποίησις ἀβλαβής; Def. 415c, my trans.). As we have seen, this meaning fits 2 Chron. 14:12 LXX, which describes how King Asa and his people routed the Ethiopians “so that there was no preservation among them” (ὥστε μὴ εἶναι ἐν αὐτοῖς περιποίησιν; NETS). Hebrews 10:39 can carry this meaning, as the NRSV translators seem to have recognized with their rendering: “We are not among those who shrink back and so are lost, but among those who have faith and so are saved.”[14] The italicized phrase is εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς, literally, “for the preservation of the life.” This meaning also works well for 1 Thess. 5:9, although no translations adopt it and commentators do not discuss the possibility—“God did not appoint [ἔθετο] us for wrath but for the preservation which is salvation [εἰς περιποίησιν σωτηρίας] through our Lord Jesus Christ.”[15] It even works well in 1 Pet. 2:9, where Peter describes Christians as a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, which might be rendered “a people destined for preservation.” These people stand in contrast to unbelievers, who are destined (ἐτέθησαν, 2:8) for disobedience and, presumably, condemnation. In Mal. 3:17 LXX, on which 1 Pet. 2:9 is based, the context is also one in which the Lord distinguishes between the righteous and the wicked on a future day of reckoning, and it is the righteous among his people who will be for him on that day a περιποίησιν. Here too the meaning “a saved remnant” fits well.[16]

Whatever we think of the plausibility of this meaning for Mal. 3:17; 1 Thess. 5:9; and 1 Pet. 2:9, it solves the problem of ambiguity in Eph. 1:14 and fits well the broader context of the letter. In 1:13–14, as we have seen, Paul describes his readers as a people who have been sealed, a metaphor that is often used in eschatological contexts to refer to God’s protection of the remnant among his people at the time of his judgment. They were sealed, Paul says, when they heard “the word of truth” and believed “the gospel of salvation.” If sealing means protection from God’s eschatological wrath, then salvation in this context means rescue from that wrath. If these ideas form the backdrop to Paul’s language here, then translating εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως “for the redemption of the saved remnant” makes good sense. We no longer need to debate whether the term refers to redemption as an eschatological “acquisition” of believers or to God’s people as his “possession.” Paul simply says that the Spirit seals believers for salvation so that “those who are saved” might receive redemption.

This interpretation receives some confirmation in 5:6, where Paul, albeit unconsciously, provides a negative counterpart to it. There Paul warns his readers that they should “let no one deceive you with empty talk: because of these things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience” (5:6). The deception of empty words here stands in contrast to the “the word of truth” that Paul’s readers have believed in 1:13, and the wrath of God coming to the disobedient who participate in such deception stands in contrast to the salvation and redemption that belong to the περιποίησις of 1:14.





II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)


III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

Personal letters in the Greco-Roman world often included a prayer report after the greeting. Sometimes this report was a thanksgiving to the gods, or to a particular god, for the well-being of the letter’s authors or recipients.[1] “I give thanks to all the gods if you are in good health yourself and everything else has been satisfactory,” says “Dromon” to “Zenon” in a short letter from the mid-third century BC (Hunt and Edgar 1932: 273). About a century later, the author of 2 Maccabees recorded an official letter from the leadership of Judea to the Jewish philosopher Aristobulus that began with a thanksgiving prayer report: “Having been saved by God out of grave dangers we thank him greatly for taking our side against the king” (1:11 NRSV).

Frequently in personal letters an intercessory prayer report follows the greeting, and nearly always these are prayers for the well-being of the recipient. “Before all I pray for your health,” reports one letter writer. Another says, “I pray always for your health; every day I make supplication for you before the lord Serapis.” Still another, “Before everything I pray for your health and that of my brothers, unharmed by the evil eye, and withal I make supplication for you daily before the lord Serapis.”[2] Sometimes ancient Greek letters used both a thanksgiving and an intercessory prayer report after the greeting, and these reports sometimes anticipated the primary theme of the letter.[3]

The letters in the NT Pauline letter corpus often follow this same general pattern. After the greeting, they commonly turn to a thanksgiving prayer report,[4] and this is sometimes followed by an intercessory prayer report.[5] These reports always anticipate important themes developed in the letter body (Schubert 1939: 180; O’Brien 1977: 262, 271).

Within the Pauline corpus itself, however, the prayer patterns vary widely (see especially O’Brien 1977). In 1 Thessalonians, a reasonable case can be made that, aside from the opening greeting, the thanksgiving prayer report covers the entire first three chapters. This massive thanksgiving report then concludes not merely with an intercessory prayer report but also with an actual intercessory prayer (3:11–13). Second Thessalonians looks similar, but instead of a long thanksgiving section, it has two discrete thanksgiving prayer reports (1:3–4 and 2:13–15), the second of which ends, as in 1 Thessalonians, with an intercessory prayer (2:16–17). In 2 Corinthians, Paul replaces the thanksgiving prayer report with a benediction (1:3–4); after digressing from prayer into a reflection on his suffering in Asia, he concludes the letter opening with a reference to the Corinthians’ intercessory prayer for him and eventual thanksgiving to God after he answers their prayers on his behalf (1:11). In Colossians, the intercessory prayer report includes a petition that the Colossians give thanks to God (1:11b–12).

It should come as no surprise, therefore, that the prayer pattern at the opening of Ephesians also demonstrates a unique combination of formal elements. Among the Pauline Letters, only Ephesians begins with a benediction, a thanksgiving prayer report, and an intercessory prayer report.[6] The combination of a thanksgiving and intercessory prayer report is reminiscent of Phil. 1:3–11; Col. 1:3–5; and Philem. 4–5. The inclusion of a benediction is reminiscent of 2 Cor. 1:3–4. At the level of form, Eph. 1:3–23 probably comes closest to 2 Cor. 1:3–4, 11, where all three elements (benediction, thanksgiving, intercession) also appear, although the subjects and order of the intercessory and thanksgiving elements are reversed (2 Cor. 1:11). At the level of Paul’s use of the prayer report form, Ephesians resembles 1 Thessalonians most closely. In both letters, the first major section alternates between prayer and descriptive material (1 Thess. 1:2–3; 2:13; 3:9; Eph. 1:3–14, 15–19; 3:1, 14–19) and then concludes with prayer (1 Thess. 3:11–13; Eph. 3:20–21).

As is common with Paul’s letters, it is difficult to tell in Ephesians precisely where the thanksgiving prayer report ends and the intercessory prayer report begins. Paul says he does not cease giving thanks for the letters’ recipients when he remembers them in prayer (1:16), but when he describes his prayers in the following subordinate clause, they turn out to be prayers not of thanksgiving but of intercession (1:17–19).

It is also hard to know where the intercessory prayer report ends and the body of the letter begins. The lengthy relative clause that runs from 1:20 to 1:21 is subordinate to Paul’s prayer in 1:19 that his readers might understand the great power of God, but it is so long that it seems to leave behind the prayer report and to merge at some point with the main body of the letter. Since Paul returns to prayer in 3:1 and 3:14–21, it seems likely that he did not wish to distinguish carefully between the prayer report and the letter body. In the first major section of the letter (1:3–3:21), he instead moves so easily between actual prayers (1:3–14; 3:1, 14–19; 3:20–21), prayer reports (1:15–19), and theological description (1:20–2:22; 3:2–13) that it becomes difficult to define the literary pattern of the first three chapters in formal, epistolary terms.[7]

Paul’s primary concern in 1:15–23 is easier to identify. He begins with a brief report of thanks to God for the “faith” (πίστις, pistis) and “love” (ἀγάπη, agapē) of the letter’s readers (1:15). As is typical of Paul’s thanksgiving prayer reports, the mention of faith and love in this part of the letter anticipates the dominant concerns of each major section of the letter. Most of the occurrences of the terms πίστις, πιστός (pistos, faithful), and πιστεύω (pisteuō, I believe) appear in 1:1–3:21, and most of the occurrences of the terms ἀγάπη, ἀγαπητός (agapētos, beloved), and ἀγαπάω (agapaō, I love) appear in 4:1–6:20.[8]

Thanksgiving yields to intercession in 1:16b, and Paul becomes more specific about his concerns. He prays that God might open the eyes of his readers’ hearts to the hope of God’s calling, to their status as God’s valuable inheritance, and especially to the immense power that God put into effect for all believers. The first and second petitions of the intercessory prayer report in verse 18 reach back to the benediction. The theme of hope recalls the mention of believers’ hope there, the theme of calling is reminiscent of the predestinarian language (vv. 4–5, 11; cf. Rom. 8:28–30), and the theme of inheritance recalls the language of adoption (v. 5) and inheritance (v. 11).

The much longer third petition (v. 19) and the complex relative clause that is attached to it (vv. 20–21) introduce Paul’s chief concern in the intercessory prayer report. Paul wants God to open his readers’ inner eyes (v. 18) to the work God has accomplished on their behalf through Christ (v. 19). He alludes to Pss. 110:1 and 8:6 to say that God has given Christ victory over all the inimical spiritual beings in the universe, and that he has given Christ, in his capacity as victor, to the church (vv. 20–22). The church, moreover, is Christ’s body and therefore full of Christ, who is full of God (v. 23).

Here Paul anticipates four major themes of the subsequent letter. First, he foreshadows the theme of the church’s defeat of the inimical spiritual powers in 2:2, 6; and 3:10 and the military and biblical expressions of that victory in 4:8 (Ps. 68:18) and 6:10–17 (Isa. 11:4–5; 52:7; and 59:17). Second, he anticipates his use of the body metaphor for the church in 2:16; 3:6; 4:4, 11–16; 5:22–33. Third, the idea that the church is full of Christ, who is full of God (v. 23), reappears in Paul’s claim that God dwells within the ethnically unified church in 2:21–22, that Christ dwells within believers’ hearts in 3:17, and that believers are full of God in 3:19. Fourth, he anticipates the theme, already broached in the benediction (1:10–11), that God is powerfully at work in his people to accomplish his purposes for the unity of the universe (3:7, 20).

In sum, the thanksgiving and intercessory prayer report turn out to be an important guide to Paul’s primary concerns in the letter. In the thanksgiving prayer report, Paul tells his readers that he is thankful for their faith in the gospel and for the love that represents the outworking of this faith. In broad terms, the rest of the letter is an exploration of the blessings that come to those who have faith in the gospel (1:3–3:21) and the love that believers should show toward one another (4:1–6:20). In the same way, the intercessory prayer report gradually moves into the main subject of the letter and both recapitulates and anticipates the letter’s most prominent themes: God’s gracious inclusion of the letter’s readers among his people by means of their faith in and relationship with Christ (1:3–14; 2:11–22; 3:2–12) and the availability of God’s immense power to his people to enable them both to defeat their cosmic enemies (2:1–3; 6:10–20) and to accomplish their important role in God’s purposes for his creation (2:10, 15; 3:10; 4:13).





III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

A. Thanksgiving for Faith and Love, and Intercession for Illumination (1:15–19)

B. God’s Great Power Displayed in Christ and for the Church (1:20–23)


A. Thanksgiving for Faith and Love, and Intercession for Illumination (1:15–19)

In the first part of his thanksgiving and intercessory prayer report, Paul tells his readers that what he has heard about them has led him to unceasing thanksgiving for them whenever he remembers them in prayer. He has heard that they have placed their faith in the gospel and that they are therefore “in the Lord Jesus” (v. 15; cf. vv. 13–14). In particular, he is grateful to hear this because, as he will explain later, God has entrusted him with the special responsibility of proclaiming to the Gentiles that they have been included in the people of God through the gospel (3:2–13). The report of his Gentile readers’ faith in the Lord Jesus and of their working out of this faith in love for their fellow believers is therefore appropriate cause for many prayers of thanksgiving (v. 16).

The real burden of this section, however, comes in the form of Paul’s intercessory prayer report, which emerges almost imperceptibly out of Paul’s expressions of thanks. Paul tells his readers that when he prays for them, he asks God that he might give the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to them. This is not a prayer for wisdom generally but specifically for wisdom related to knowing God (v. 17).

Paul prays, moreover, that this revelation about God might come to the letter’s readers as God illumines their inner self (“the eyes of your heart”) about three theological truths (v. 18a). Paul expresses these truths in three clauses, each beginning with a form of the interrogative pronoun “what” (τίς, tis). He prays that God will grant his readers insight into (1) the hope they have as a result of God’s call to be his people (v. 18b), (2) the rich glory they possess in their status as God’s own inheritance (v. 18c), and (3) the enormity of the power that God has put into effect for their advantage (v. 19).

This series of three clauses grows in complexity as it progresses. The first clause (v. 18b) is a simple construction in Greek and contains no explicit reference to God’s people; such a reference is only implied in the action nouns “hope” and “calling,” whose subjects must be the immediately preceding “you.” The second clause (v. 18c) moves a step beyond this to make explicit reference to God’s people in the concluding prepositional phrase “in the saints.” The third clause (v. 19) makes an even more explicit reference to God’s people with the longer prepositional phrase “toward us who believe” and the shift from the second-person plural “you” (v. 18a) to the more-inclusive first-person plural “we.” In addition, this final clause includes a second prepositional phrase that describes God’s power with an elaborate genitive construction.

The length and complexity of this third indefinite clause, and the further elaboration of it in 1:20–23, reveal that this clause contains Paul’s primary concern in his intercessory prayers for his readers. It also anticipates an important theme of the entire letter.



Exegesis and Exposition

15Because of this, I in particular, after hearing of your faith in the Lord Jesus and ⌜love⌝ for all the saints, 16do not cease giving thanks for you when remembering you in my prayers 17that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, ⌜might give⌝ to you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, 18ahaving the eyes of your heart enlightened in order that you might know 18bwhat is the hope of his calling, 18cwhat is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, 19and what is the surpassing greatness of his power for us who believe, according to the effect of the might of his strength, . . .

[1:15–16] The beginning of Paul’s thanksgiving prayer report has seemed unclear to some readers. Does διὰ τοῦτο (dia touto, because of this) point backward (most commentators and translations) or forward (NRSV)? Is it perhaps a light rather than logical connective phrase, merely intended to keep the discourse flowing (Best 1998: 158)? If it points backward, does it refer back to the whole benediction (vv. 3–14; e.g., Schnackenburg 1991: 72), only to the last section with its reference to the readers’ conversion (vv. 13–14; e.g., Ellicott 1859: 20), or to the whole benediction but with the readers themselves now particularly in mind (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 54)? Moreover, what are we to make of the term κἀγώ (kagō) in this context? Although Paul frequently uses the first-person singular in his thanksgiving prayer reports (1 Cor. 1:4; Phil. 1:3; Rom. 1:8; Philem. 4; cf. 1 Tim. 1:12; 2 Tim. 1:3), he never uses the emphatic pronoun ἐγώ (egō, I) or the contraction κἀγώ (καί + ἐγώ, kai+ egō, also + I) with the verb of thanksgiving.

In this diction some commentators have found hints of a hand other than Paul’s. Διὰ τοῦτο κἀγώ seems to be borrowed from διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡμεῖς (dia touto kai hēmeis, because of this we also) in Col. 1:9 (e.g., Muddiman 2001: 82; Sellin 2008: 124). The unusual κἀγώ, moreover, fits with the emphasis in Ephesians on the authority of the great apostle Paul himself (cf. 3:1 and 4:1), an emphasis that most likely comes from an admirer (Lincoln 1990: 54; cf. Hübner 1997: 145).

The phrase, however, is certainly within Paul’s stylistic repertoire: it occurs word for word in 1 Thess. 3:5. The emphasis on Paul’s apostolic authority, moreover, does not accent that authority generally, but a specific element of Paul’s call to be an apostle. God has graciously given to him the role of proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles (3:1, 8), and in this role he has met with suffering, including the imprisonment he experiences as he writes this letter (3:13; 4:1; 6:20). First-person comments on this element of Paul’s apostolic call are not unusual within the undisputed Pauline letters (Rom. 11:13–14; 15:14–16, 31).

This theme that God had granted Paul a special gift of proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles (3:8) may hold the key to understanding how the thanksgiving prayer report and the benediction are related to each other. The phrase διὰ τοῦτο points backward to Paul’s description in verses 13–14 of the conversion of his readers after they have heard the gospel, and the term κἀγώ refers to Paul’s particular interest, as the apostle to the Gentiles, in their conversion. Because his readers have heard and believed the gospel and have been sealed with the Holy Spirit, Paul says, “I in particular” have reason to give unceasing thanks in my prayers.[1]

Paul began thanking God for his readers after he heard (ἀκούσας, akousas) of their faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints. In this reference only to “hearing” of his readers’ faith and love, some commentators see a sign that the letter cannot have been addressed to Ephesus (e.g., E. Scott 1930: 152) or is pseudepigraphic (e.g., Sellin 2008: 124).[2] Assuming that Paul really did address the letter to Christians in Ephesus, where, according to Acts, he had spent between two and three years (Acts 19:8, 10; 20:31), talk of only hearing of his readers’ faith and love with no mention of his personal relationship to them seems odd. The oddity only deepens with further hints later in the letter that Paul and his readers have little personal knowledge of each other (3:2; 4:21; 6:21–24).

These expressions of distance from his readers are more natural, however, if Paul wrote Ephesians after an absence from the city of over seven years and near the end of almost five years of imprisonment (Acts 24:27; 27:9; 28:11, 30). Much had probably changed even in the house churches that had some connection to his original ministry, and some Christians in the city had never had more than a loose connection to his ministry there (Acts 18:24–28; cf. Trebilco 2004: 115–27). By the time Paul wrote Ephesians, he could have known many, perhaps most, of his readers only by hearing of them from someone else.

The report that Paul received brought news of his readers’ πίστις (pistis, faith) and ἀγάπη (agapē, love). Both are qualities that also appear in the thanksgiving prayer reports of Colossians (1:4) and Philemon (v. 5). This could mean that someone writing in Paul’s name leaned heavily on Col. 1:4 and Philem. 5 when writing these words (e.g., Mitton 1951: 65; Gnilka 1971: 88; Lincoln 1990: 49; Hübner 1997: 144–45; Sellin 2008: 124–25). It seems at least equally likely, however, that Paul wrote Ephesians at about the same time as Colossians and Philemon and used similar language in his thanksgiving prayer reports in each letter. A close comparison of the three letters at this point reveals exactly the kind of agreement in substance but difference in specific wording that one would expect if a single author wrote all three letters at about the same time but with no concern to repeat the wording of one letter in another. At the same time, the small differences in wording between the three are not what one would expect if the author of Ephesians were trying to follow Colossians.[3]

First, Paul gives thanks for the faith that his readers have placed ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ (en tō kyriō Iēsou, in the Lord Jesus). Grammatically, this phrase could mean either that the Lord Jesus is the object of his readers’ faith (that they have placed their trust in him) or that the Lord Jesus is the sphere of his readers’ faith (that they exercise faith as people who are “in Christ”). In ancient Jewish and Christian literature, words that refer to believing and to faith sometimes express the object of that faith with an ἐν clause (e.g., Ps. 105:12 LXX [106:12 MT, Eng.]; Jer. 12:6 LXX; Sir. 32:21; Mark 1:15; John 3:15; Ign. Phld. 8.2), but when faith terminology together with an ἐν clause that has Christ Jesus as its object shows up in the Pauline corpus, the construction most often describes the sphere in which faith operates (Gal. 5:6; 1 Tim. 1:14; 3:13; 2 Tim. 1:13; 3:15; Lincoln 1990: 55). In 1:1 and 13 Paul had used the phrases πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (pistois en Christō Iēsou, believers, in Christ Jesus) and ἐν ᾧ . . . πιστεύσαντες (en hō . . . pisteusantes, in whom . . . , when you believed) respectively to refer to the sphere in which his readers had exercised their faith, and this, together with the typical Pauline usage, probably means that Paul had the sphere rather than the object of his readers’ faith uppermost in mind here also (Lincoln 1990: 55).

Still, we should be careful not to make the separation between sphere and object too watertight. If Paul wrote the thanksgiving prayer report in Philemon at roughly the same time that he composed the prayer reports in Colossians and Ephesians, then the distinction seems to be relatively unimportant to him. In Philem. 5 he unambiguously gives thanks that his readers have put their faith in Christ (τὴν πίστιν, ἣν ἔχεις πρὸς τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν, tēn pistin, hēn echeis pros ton kyrion Iēsoun, the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus). It would be very difficult to make a convincing case that something in the historical context of Philemon drove Paul to emphasize the object of his readers’ faith whereas something in the context of Col. 1:4 or Eph. 1:15 led him to emphasize the sphere of their faith. Paul probably thought he was saying roughly the same thing in each of the three letters, and so here in Eph. 1:15 Paul probably intends to affirm both that his readers trusted Christ and that they are in Christ by faith.

Paul also gives thanks for “the love” his readers have “for all the saints” (ἡ ἀγάπη ἡ εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους, hē agapē hē eis pantas tous hagious). Ἅγιοι (hagioi, saints) here, as usual in Ephesians, refers to all Christians (1:18; 3:8, 18; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18), and love is a theme of particular interest to Paul in this letter: God’s love for believers (2:4; 3:17; 6:23), Christ’s love for believers (3:19), the love of believers for Christ (6:24), and especially the love of believers for each other (1:4; 4:2, 15, 16; 5:2, 25, 28, 33). Just as he does elsewhere in his opening thanksgiving prayer reports, therefore, Paul congratulates his readers for displaying precisely the quality that he will urge them later in the letter to cultivate.[4]

[1:17] The ἵνα that begins verse 17 introduces the content of his prayers for his readers.[5] They are prayers not only of thanksgiving for their faith and love but also of intercession. Paul begins his description of the intercessory element of his prayers with a twofold description of God, both parts of which echo the letter’s opening benediction.

First, the God to whom Paul prays is ὁ θεὸς τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (ho theos tou kuriou hēmōn Iēsou Christou, the God of our Lord Jesus Christ), just as he is in the benediction (1:3). As with the benediction, so with the intercessory prayer report, the phrase demonstrates the centrality of Jesus Christ to God’s purposes.

Second, God is also ὁ πατήρ (ho patēr, the Father), just as in the benediction (cf. Rom. 15:6; 2 Cor. 1:3; 11:31; 1 Pet. 1:3), but now, rather than the Father of Jesus, he is ὁ πατὴρ τῆς δόξης (ho patēr tēs doxēs, the Father of glory).[6] Here Paul uses the term “Father” metaphorically to mean that the God to whom he prays is the origin and defining example of glory. The expression resembles 2 Cor. 1:3, where God is the “Father” of mercies, and James 1:17, where he is the “Father” of lights (Best 1998: 161). The glory that God displays is the splendor or brightness that is often characteristic of God’s power, authority, and honor in the OT and that he graciously shares with his people (HALOT 1:457–58; BDAG 257).[7] As the benediction has shown, it is for the praise of God’s glory (1:12, 14), shown especially in his grace (1:6), that God has made his people heirs (1:12) and provided them with a future inheritance (1:14).

Paul prays that this glorious God, who has shown his grace to his people in Jesus Christ, might give to his readers πνεῦμα σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως (pneuma sophias kai apokalypseōs, the Spirit of wisdom and revelation). Is Paul praying here that God might give to his readers a “disposition” of wisdom and revelation (see, e.g., Abbott 1897: 28; Westcott 1906: 22; Swete 1909: 234)? He can certainly use the term πνεῦμα in this way in other places, speaking sometimes of “a spirit of gentleness” (πνεύμα . . . πραΰτητος, pneuma . . . praytētos, 1 Cor. 4:21; cf. Gal. 6:1), “a spirit of slavery” (πνεῦμα δουλείας, pneuma douleias, Rom. 8:15), or “a spirit of cowardice” (πνεῦμα δειλίας, pneuma deilias, 2 Tim. 1:7).[8] Here in Ephesians he can refer in a similar way to “the spirit of your mind” (τὸ πνεύμα τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, to pneuma tou noös hymōn, 4:23), and there is precedent for the use of the phrase πνεῦμα σοφίας in this way in the OT and other Jewish literature extant during Paul’s era (e.g., Deut. 34:9; Wis. 7:7).

The trouble for this reading comes with the genitive ἀποκαλύψεως. What could Paul mean by a “spirit of revelation”? Since God is the one who gives revelation to people, the phrase seems virtually unintelligible as a reference to the human spirit (Fee 1994: 676; Best 1998: 163). In addition, the only other place in Ephesians where the term πνεῦμα and the concept of “revelation” come together is 3:4–5, and there God’s Spirit reveals “the mystery of Christ” to apostles and prophets (ἀπεκαλύφθη τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις ἐν πνεύματι, apekalyphthē tois hagiois apostolois autou kai prophētais en pneumati; cf. Lincoln 1990: 57). These considerations weigh heavily in favor of taking πνεῦμα here in 1:17 as a reference to God’s Spirit. Paul is saying that he asks God in prayer to give his readers “the Spirit of wisdom and revelation.”[9]

This understanding of the phrase, however, also encounters a problem: Paul has just emphasized that his readers have already been sealed with the Holy Spirit (1:13). If this is so, then in what meaningful sense can Paul pray that God might give them the Spirit (Swete 1909: 234)? This is a real interpretive difficulty, but since Paul so clearly connects God’s Spirit with revelation elsewhere in the letter, it seems most likely that, despite this difficulty, he refers to God’s Spirit here. If this is correct, then Paul requests not that God would give the Spirit to his readers for the first time but that God would awaken them to the Spirit’s role of revealing wisdom and revelation to them (cf. Fee 1994: 676n55).

Paul makes explicit the theocentric aspect of both the wisdom and the revelation that he prays God would give his readers with the phrase ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ (en epignōsei autou, in the knowledge of him). Some interpreters have thought this clause gives the means “by” which the wisdom and revelation come (e.g., Haupt 1902a: 36), and others have attached it to the first part of verse 18 so that Paul prays for the enlightenment of his readers “in the knowledge of him” (e.g., Abbott 1897: 28). The most natural reading grammatically and contextually, however, takes it as a description of the sphere of knowledge with which Paul’s prayers are concerned (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 23–24; Hoehner 2002: 259). He prays not for knowledge generally but that God’s Spirit, who reveals wisdom and understanding to God’s people, might reveal the knowledge of God to the believers who read this letter.[10]

[1:18a] Paul continues his prayer report with a phrase whose grammar is difficult to construe. He clearly refers to the enlightenment of his readers’ inner being, but is this a further request in addition to the gift of the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, or does the enlightenment of the inner being in some way describe how that gift will be given? Since the participle πεφωτισμένους (pephōtismenous, enlightening) is accusative, we might at first think that it supplies a second direct object, in addition to the πνεῦμα of verse 17, for the verb δώῃ (dōē, may give). Paul would then be praying that that his readers would receive (1) the gift of the Spirit of wisdom and revelation and (2) the gift of enlightenment (e.g., Best 1998: 164–65). If this were Paul’s meaning, however, we would expect a καί (kai, also) before πεφωτισμένους to make clear that he wanted it to function as the beginning of a clause that names the second direct object of δώῃ (Lincoln 1990: 47).

It is more likely, therefore, that πεφωτισμένους modifies δώῃ adverbially and describes what will happen when God gives the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to Paul’s readers: the eyes of their heart will be enlightened. This enlightenment will, in turn, prepare them to know the hope of God’s calling (v. 18b), the immense glory of his inheritance among the saints (v. 18c), and the massive power he has used for the benefit of believers (v. 19).

If this is the correct reading of πεφωτισμένους, however, why is it in the accusative rather than the dative case? Normal rules of Greek syntax lead us to expect that the case of the participle will agree with the case of its subject, and in this instance the subject of πεφωτισμένους is the dative ὑμῖν that precedes it. The nineteenth-century grammarian G. B. Winer offered a satisfactory explanation for this long ago. “If a sentence is continued by means of participles,” he observed, “these, when at a distance from the governing verb, not unfrequently [sic] assume an abnormal case.”[11] In this instance, πεφωτισμένους has assumed the accusative case because it is a long way from the main verb δώῃ with its object ὑμῖν and because in the purpose clause for which πεφωτισμένους prepares the way, the case of ὑμῖν switches to the accusative form ὑμᾶς.

When Paul speaks of the enlightenment of the eyes of his readers’ hearts, he uses imagery that was common in both the Greco-Roman and Jewish worlds for gaining religious knowledge and insight. Ovid describes a mystic from Samos who could not see the gods with his physical eyes but “still approached them with his thought” and “feasted” on them “with the inner eye” (oculis ea pectoris; Metam. 15.60; TNTGH 2.1:596). In the Corpus hermeticum (4.11b; cf. 7.1a) Hermes tells his son Tat that he should gaze “with the eyes of your heart” (τοῖς τῆς καρδίας ὀφθαλμοῖς, tois tēs kardias ophthalmois) on the likeness of God that Hermes has painted for him in his discourse.[12] The Qumran Community Rule instructs the priests to bless the community with the prayer that God may “illuminate your heart with the discernment of life” (1QS 2.3, trans. García Martínez and Tigchelaar 1997).

Later Paul will speak of his readers’ conversion as a movement from darkness to light (5:8–14; cf. 4:18, 20; Col. 1:13). Here in 1:18a, however, he probably does not have in mind his readers’ conversion (pace Lincoln 1990: 58), still less their baptism (pace Schlier 1957: 80–81). Instead, he is thinking of the work of God’s Spirit within his readers to help them understand both what God intends for them as his people and the power that God has made available to them.

[1:18b] Paul expresses the content of the knowledge that he prays his readers will gain in three indefinite clauses, each more elaborate than the one preceding it. The first two of these clauses pick up themes that appeared in the benediction. The final clause (in v. 19), separated from the first two by καί, introduces the new theme of the mighty power of God that is available to Paul’s readers in the present. Paul will explain this theme more fully in the long relative clause and concluding sentence of the intercessory prayer report (vv. 20–23).

First, Paul prays that his readers will understand the ἐλπίς (elpis, hope) that God’s κλῆσις (klēsis, calling) gives them. In the NT, the concept of “calling” is especially characteristic of the Pauline literature (BDAG 549; Schmidt, TDNT 3:491–92), which makes clear that the believer’s call comes at God’s initiative and stands in close connection with God’s sovereign choice of his people (Rom. 11:29). It originates, therefore, in God’s grace and prior decision (Rom. 8:28–30; 2 Tim. 1:9). Those who are called must, nevertheless, live in a way that is worthy of this calling (2 Thess. 1:11), and their calling will be fully realized only in the future (Phil. 3:14). The concept appears three times in Ephesians, once here in 1:18 and then again in 4:1 and 4:4. These three occurrences mesh neatly with the use of the idea elsewhere in the Pauline literature. In 1:18 and 4:4 “calling” is connected with hope, emphasizing its future fulfillment, and in 4:1 Paul admonishes his readers that they must walk in a way that is worthy of the calling they have received.

The calling of God, Paul says, gives rise to ἐλπίς. For Paul, “hope” does not involve an uncertain expectation that things might turn out well, but a firm conviction, against all appearances to the contrary (Rom. 4:16–18), that God will be gracious to his people because of what he has already accomplished for them in Christ (Rom. 5:5; cf. Eph. 1:12; 2:12–13). In Colossians, Paul is so certain that the Christian’s hope will be realized that he can describe it as in some sense already laid up for believers in heaven (1:5; cf. 1 Pet. 1:3). When Paul speaks of “the hope of [God’s] calling” here in 1:18b, therefore, he describes something that, although future and therefore invisible, arises from God’s call and is bound to happen (cf. Rom. 8:24–25). Paul’s readers have this hope (1:12), but Paul prays that the Spirit will illumine the eyes of their heart so that they might see it clearly.

[1:18c] Second, Paul prays God would give his readers an understanding of their status as God’s very glorious inheritance. In the benediction Paul has already said that his readers, as God’s adopted children, are his heirs (1:5, 11) and have been sealed with the Holy Spirit as a down payment of their coming inheritance (1:14). Now we learn that God too has an inheritance, and it is his people﻿[13]—οἱ ἅγιοι (hoi hagioi, the saints), as Paul calls them (cf. 1:1, 15; 2:19; 3:8, 18; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18).[14] In a similar way, the benediction had emphasized the glory of God and of his grace (1:6, 12, 14), and Paul has just described God as the Father, or origin, of glory (1:17). Now we learn that believers too are glorious; indeed, they have a wealth of glory.[15] Paul wants his readers to know, therefore, that they are of great value to God: they are rich in glory and they are his inheritance.[16]

[1:19] Third, Paul prays that they will understand the vast magnitude of God’s power and that God has put this power into effect for the advantage of all believers. He lends solemnity and emphasis to this thought by piling up words for power in two phrases.

In the first phrase, he refers not simply to God’s power but to τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ (to hyperballon megethos tēs dynameōs autou, the surpassing greatness of his power). The term ὑπερβάλλον means “surpassing,” “outstripping,” “excelling,” “exceeding all bounds,” and even, in a negative sense, “overbidding,” “excessive” (LSJ 1860). Μέγεθος (megethos) can simply denote “magnitude,” “size,” or “height” (LSJ 1089), and this is its most frequent meaning in the LXX (1 Sam. 16:7; 1 Kings 6:23; 7:21; 2 Kings 19:23; Ezek. 19:11; 31:3, 5, 10, 14). Often, however, the term means “greatness” or “strength” with the connotation that the measurement of the strength to which it refers is very great (cf. BDAG 624–25). It appears twice in the LXX in prayers that God would use the “might” or “strength” of his arm to defeat the enemies of his people (Exod. 15:16; 2 Macc. 15:24), and as the context will show (Eph. 1:20–23), this is the sense in which Paul thinks of God’s might here. Paul therefore could simply have spoken of “the greatness of his power” (τὸ μέγεθος τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ), but he wanted to place special emphasis on the enormous size of God’s power and so instead says that God’s power is surpassingly great.

The second phrase is a prepositional construction that begins with κατά (kata, according to) and its object ἐνέργειαν (energeian, effect) and then further qualifies ἐνέργειαν with two synonyms for this word in the genitive case. The whole phrase qualifies the term δυνάμεως and describes the norm against which the “surpassing greatness” of God’s “power” should be measured.[17] God’s power should be calculated κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ (kata tēn energeian tou kratous tēs ischyos autou, according to the effect of the might of his strength). Greek philosophers distinguished between δύναμις (dynamis), which they understood as potentiality or capacity, and ἐνέργεια (energeia), which they viewed as the outworking of this potentiality (Urmson 1990: 47). In the rest of the letter, there is some evidence that Paul distinguished between the two terms in a similar way when he used them together (3:7, 20; cf. Col. 1:29), and such a distinction fits well here. We should keep in mind, however, that Paul is probably also preparing for his statement in 1:21 that God has placed Christ over every δύναμις, meaning a powerful being. There it will become clear that God’s subjection of the δυνάμεις (dynameis, powers) to Christ is one way in which his own δύναμις (potential power) has become ἐνέργεια (effective power).

It is also possible to assign distinct meanings to κράτος (kratos) and ἰσχύς (ischys) and then to think of Paul as saying something like “the potential power of God can be measured by the norm of the effective power of his inherent ability to overcome resistance.”[18] We probably do more justice to Paul’s intentions in this complex genitive construction, however, if we resist the temptation to parse the logic of the phrase and the meaning of its terms precisely. Where the phrase “the might of his power” or something similar appears elsewhere in Jewish and early Christian literature, it is simply a full way of speaking of the greatness of God’s power (cf. 1QS 11.19–20; 1QHa 12.32; 23.8; Isa. 40:25–26 LXX; 1 Clem. 27.5), and that is probably how we should take the similar phrase here.[19] Paul wants his readers to understand the magnitude of God’s power, and he prays that God might open his readers’ eyes to this spiritual reality.

Paul’s ultimate purpose in describing the greatness of God’s power, however, is to inform his readers that this power is εἰς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πιστεύοντας (eis hēmas tous pisteuontas, for us who believe). He uses εἰς in this phrase as a substitute for the dative of advantage: God’s power, he says, is for the advantage of believers (BDAG 290). Paul’s sudden switch from the second-person-plural “you” (vv. 16, 17, 18) to the first-person-plural “we/us” emphasizes the inclusiveness of this thought; there are no exceptions. God has placed at the disposal of all believers, both Paul and his readers, the great power that Paul has just described in general terms (Best 1998: 168). Now, in verses 20–23 he will show his readers precisely how God has exercised his great power on their behalf.

Summary

In 1:15–19 Paul’s praise of God for the salvation of his readers through their hearing and believing the gospel gives way to thanksgiving to God for the report Paul has heard of their sound commitment to the gospel. This thought, in turn, becomes intercession on their behalf. Paul’s thanksgiving was motivated by his particular interest, as apostle to the Gentiles, in the genuineness of his Gentile readers’ conversion. His intercession for them was probably motivated by their discouragement (3:13) and is Paul’s primary concern in his prayer report. Paul’s intercessory prayer for his readers focuses on his request that the Spirit might reveal the knowledge of God to them. He is concerned that they understand, in particular, three theological truths: (1) that they have a firm hope for a bright, eternal future because God has called them to be his people; (2) that, as God’s people, they are his glorious inheritance; and (3) that God has put his vast power into effect for their benefit.
