Paul is especially concerned that God should grant his readers an understanding of this third theological truth, which is so important that Paul explains it further in an elaborate relative clause (1:20–23) that concludes his intercessory prayer report and that we will examine in the next section.



Additional Notes

1:15. The question of whether Paul included a reference to love in verse 15 or spoke only of faith in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints is one of the letter’s more difficult textual problems. The earliest and best witnesses to the letter’s text omit the reference to love and have only τὴν καθ’ ὑμᾶς πίστιν ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους. These include 𝔓46, א, A, B, P, 33, 1739, 1881, 2464, Origen, Jerome (who followed Origen’s commentary closely), and a number of Bohairic witnesses.

This reading is also the most difficult to understand and therefore can explain most easily how the construction τὴν καθ’ ὑμᾶς πίστιν ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους arose. Scribes who were puzzled by what “faith toward all the saints” might mean may have relied on Col. 1:4 (ἀκούσαντες τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην ἣν ἔχετε εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους) and Philem. 5 (ἀκούων σου τὴν ἀγάπην καὶ τὴν πίστιν, ἣν ἔχεις πρὸς τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν καὶ εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους) to reshape Eph. 1:15 so that it too referred to both faith in the Lord Jesus and love toward all the saints. The reading in the minuscule manuscripts 81, 104, 326, 365, and 1175 (τὴν ἀγάπην εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους), and the reading in the uncials D, F, and G (τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους ἀγάπην), may be even more stylistically pleasing attempts to accomplish the same goal. Best (1998: 169) was convinced by this evidence and accepted the shorter reading as what Paul actually wrote (cf. Barth 1974: 146–47).

The problem with this otherwise sensible approach becomes clear when we try to interpret the phrase τὴν καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς πίστιν ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους. The grammar is clear enough: the second τήν puts the prepositional phrase εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους into the attributive position with respect to πίστιν, and so the phrase refers to the readers’ faith. This faith, then, is both “in the Lord Jesus” and “toward all the saints.” Is Paul saying that his readers exercise faith toward all the saints?

So far in Ephesians, πίστις has always referred to the trust that Paul’s readers have exercised in the sphere, or spiritual context, of Christ Jesus. In both 1:1 and 1:13 they have placed their trust in the gospel, and they have done this “in Christ Jesus” or “in Christ.” The first reference to faith in the short text of 1:15 fits perfectly within this understanding of faith: Paul has heard of the trust that his readers have placed in the gospel as people who are “in the Lord Jesus” (cf. Col. 1:4a). If we accept this as the proper understanding of the phrase τὴν καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς πίστιν ἐν τῷ κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ, however, then the faith that Paul’s readers have “toward all the saints” would also have to be this kind of trust. Paul would be thankful for the report that his readers trust both the gospel and one another. Unless we take Rom. 1:12 (συμπαρακληθῆναι ἐν ὑμῖν διὰ τῆς ἐν ἀλλήλοις πίστεως ὑμῶν τε καὶ ἐμοῦ) as a reference to mutual trust in one another, which is unlikely, there is no precedent in the Pauline literature for using πίστις in this way. In the New Testament and early Christian literature, πίστις in the sense of “trust, confidence, and faith” is “directed toward God and Christ, their revelations, teachings, promises, their power and readiness to aid” (BDAG 819).

Best (1998: 160) believes that we should interpret πίστις not as “trust” but as “loyalty,” and Barth (1974: 146–47) similarly thinks that we should understand πίστις here as something close to “love.” This makes good sense in itself (Paul’s readers would then be loyal both to Christ and to one another, or showing love to both Christ and one another), but it does not seem to agree with the use of faith as a concept in 1:1 and especially in the very close 1:13.

Because of this interpretive difficulty, it seems best to adopt (with some hesitation) the longer reading of the text as original. This longer reading appears in the majority of Greek manuscripts, the entire Latin tradition, the seventh-century Syriac version translated by Thomas of Harkel, the Sahidic version, and a number of Bohairic witnesses. In addition, it is the reading of the second corrector of א (working in about the seventh cent.), the first corrector of D (working in the sixth–seventh cent.), and Ψ (from the eighth–ninth cent.). Although these witnesses are neither as early nor as generally reliable as the witnesses to the shorter reading, they are numerous and geographically widespread.

How did the shorter reading arise? A scribe’s eye may have skipped from the first to the second τήν in the phrase τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους, thus leaving out the crucial terms τὴν ἀγάπην (Abbott 1897: 24; Metzger 1994: 533). The two variations of the longer reading found in 81, 104, 326, 365, and 1175 (τὴν ἀγάπην εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους) and in D, F, and G (τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους ἀγάπην) may simply be attempts to improve on the style of the longer reading by leaving out a redundant article (Metzger 1994: 533; Lincoln 1990: 47).

1:17. The form rendered δώῃ in NA27 is in the subjunctive mood. Since the ι subscript would not have appeared in the earliest texts of Ephesians, however, we might just as easily read δῴη as δώῃ. Δῴη is an optative and would lend a slightly more uncertain and formal air to Paul’s prayer report. Most grammarians and commentators reject this reading (e.g., Best 1998: 155, 162; Aletti 2001: 95n27). Moulton (MHT 1:196–97) says that by the time of the NT writers, the optative mood after a ἵνα that introduces a purpose clause (a “final” ἵνα) was becoming obsolete and would have looked “artificial,” like an attempt to resuscitate the elegance of the bygone era of Attic literary accomplishment (cf. Hoehner 2002: 255–56).

A few scholars have disagreed with the majority, although they have often not argued the case at all, or done so only briefly.[20] Several considerations, however, weigh in favor of this minority position. First, the ἵνα preceding this optative is at least as much a conjunction meaning “that” as it is the introduction to a purpose clause (BDAG 476). Second, when Paul uses the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι elsewhere in Ephesians, he always uses the form δῷ rather than δώῃ.[21] The appearance of ΔΩΗ here, therefore, probably signals a different mood, not simply a different spelling of the aorist subjunctive. Third, Paul probably uses the aorist optative of δίδωμι in Rom. 15:5, again in the context of prayer.[22] This shows that Paul felt comfortable with using the optative in prayer contexts. Fourth, in a sentence that may have been familiar to Paul from the LXX (1 Chron. 22:12), David tells his son Solomon, δῴη σοι σοφίαν καὶ σύνεσιν κύριος καὶ κατισχύσαι σε ἐπὶ Ισραηλ (“May the Lord grant you wisdom and understanding and strengthen you over Israel”; NETS).[23] Here there can be no doubt that δῴη should be read rather than δώῃ since it is paired with the optative κατισχύσαι. As with Paul’s use of the form in Eph. 1:17, moreover, the context is one of a prayer-wish, and the prayer-wish is for wisdom. For these reasons, Paul probably intended to use the aorist optative rather than the aorist subjunctive when he dictated ΔΩΗ in 1:17.
